for leave to introduce Bill C-383, to protect the indexing of payments made under the Canada Pension Plan.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. On February 27 the minister told the House of Commons that Joseph Lanza and Delbert Hickey were not reappointed to the Hamilton Harbour Commission because the government was suspicious of their ethical standards. Was the minister's decision based on information provided by the RCMP and, if so, when did he receive that information and when did he act upon it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a lot of confusion about the Hamilton port matter, not amongst hon. members, because they followed it fairly closely, but because the problem was two-fold. There was first the problem of what seemed to be internal corruption, since two persons have been condemned, and then the problem of collusion between the

companies which attempted, let us say, to defraud the government. The matter is now before the courts; I therefore can pass no judgment. Mr. Speaker, we delayed appointments because we did not know whether Messrs. Lanza and Hickey were mixed up in the first phase of the internal corruption which allegedly existed at the port of Hamilton.

subtopic: HARBOURS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister said that on February 27 these two men were not reappointed-I did not say appointed, but reappointed-because the government was suspicious about the ethical standards of these men. Was that the reason they were not reappointed and, if so, was this decision based on information received from the RCMP, when did the minister receive the information and when did he act on it? It was the minister who did not reappoint them.

subtopic: HARBOURS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me go back to what I was saying. The first steps in the case of the port of Hamilton were taken by the board itself and by the city which withdrew its representative, Mr. Elliot. However, because of the circumstances, we decided, instead of suspending them, to appoint them for only six months, to find out exactly what was going on.

speechtext: In view of the fact that Canada is losing its credibility as a supplier of grain, and also in view of the fact that the port of Seattle is stealing much of the business from the port of Vancouver, will the government undertake any new initiatives to resolve these labour problems so that we will not continue to run into these difficulties, thereby not only losing sales but also our credibility?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government, of course, is concerned about this issue and the exact initiatives being taken to attempt to lessen labour unrest in this country are more properly discussed by my colleague, the Minister of Labour. While I understand that there are those who would damage our reputation abroad by emphasizing our vulnerability, I hope the hon. member will at least recognize that other countries, like the United States and Australia, have been equally vulnerable.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, March 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-8, to establish a national petroleum company, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from Atlantic Canada, I suppose I might be accused of being parochial if I were to try to present some of the problems that exist in that area of Canada, yet I think it is absolutely necessary that for a few moments we do discuss this particular matter. When one looks at Atlantic Canada from the point of view of energy supply, one cannot help but be reminded of Bill C-8 and the total neglect and utter lack of planning on the part of the federal government of this country ever since oil became an integral part of our energy structure.
One cannot help but remember that when efforts were being made to construct oil refineries in eastern Canada, roadblocks were established, for real and artificial reasons, without any real substantiation by the Government of Canada, the result being that these refineries never were built on the sea coasts of New Brunswick or Nova Scotia to the extent they should have been.

Therefore, we in Atlantic Canada find ourselves in the position of being at the mercy of foreign oil suppliers, as well as at the mercy and whim of government if it does not see fit to pay attention to requests made of it by Atlantic Canada. It would have meant a very important industry in the area of Saint John had the government, through its Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, chosen to cut the red tape and allow construction by a very reputable company of a large refinery there. There would have followed a number of vital side industries and it would have guaranteed oil supply to the eastern half of Canada. But this was not to be the fact.
This, of course, is the point from which we start. We hear of discussions concerning a pipeline to be built from Sarnia to Montreal, but we hear nothing of discussions regarding energy supply and security of supply for Atlantic Canada. I think this indicates that the present government does not have the concern of the whole nation at heart as it plans its oil policy.
As one considers Bill C-8 it is rather interesting to examine some of the information published in Canada in the last three to five years regarding expansion of gas sales for all purposes. This information would indicate that while we had a limited supply of gas, we could never, under any circumstance, relax our efforts to search for and develop additional gas supplies in view of the limited period of time that we could supply gas for existing use. Today, no real effort is being made to take cognizance of the statistics that have been presented year after year.
In view of the limitations of supply which are statistical knowledge to the man on the street, during the past five years we have had a chaotic government creating an economic atmosphere in which the oil industry has been unable to see the end of the trail. The industry did not choose to continue on the same vigorous note that had been characteristic of the oil industry since the find at Leduc.
What we find after reading one publication after another is that there is a decline in the amount of expenditure on search for and development of this most vital ingredient of our society. For instance, one graph which was recently published showed that from 1973 until 1975 oil rig activity in this country declined by just about one-half. That, Mr. Speaker, is over a two-year period. With regard to offshore drilling, we find there has not been the same impetus as there was before chaotic government created a chaotic financial situation in which the oil companies, be they native or foreign, refused to risk the investment of their money.
Another publication reveals that the number of wells being drilled in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and the Arctic has been on the decline. Again we have only to go back three years in order to establish this very significant trend.
The financial pages, the budget, speeches that have been made by cabinet ministers, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in particular, disclose the economic reason for the absence of this activity. On the other hand, if we examine such activity abroad we find a complete contrast in those countries which have recognized that they must have oil; they have taken competitive economic steps to attract money.
Petro-Canada
Canada was considered one of the most stable economic opportunities in the world. It no longer has that reputation, nor will it ever regain it if we do not come up with plans which point in a specific direction indicating that Canada does, in fact, want to develop.
We do not have to look very far in various publications to find that in the last five years, let us say, the graph which indicates the consumption of oil in Canada has been rapidly gaining on the graph which indicates oil production in this country, and that we will no longer be self-sufficient as at the end of 1975. These were predictable and projectable items of fact which should have influenced the policy of the Government of Canada to secure our supply and to permit development and research.
We do not have to look far to see what the side effects of this situation will be. Prior to the time that Canada approached self-sufficiency of supply we found ourselves in economic imbalance as a result of trade deficits, which had a very considerable impact upon our economy. Yet while the handwriting was on the wall indicating that the same economic imbalance would be created by any decline in the production of oil or by any expansion of the importation of oil, no action was taken by the government which would have encouraged further search for and development of new sources of oil and other forms of energy. We have, instead, quibbled with our neighbour to the south as to how we would get the energy assets out of the Arctic. We have, instead, dilly-dallied, fiddle-faddled in every way possible to delay those operations which very well might have put us in a different position.
The government should have followed a few of the charts which were put out by the dailies, the weeklies, the Financial Post and by practically every source of news dissemination that exists in this country. It could, for instance, have looked at the chart which indicated to Canadians that as royalties went up, companies both national and international lost interest in the development and search for new sources of oil. The government could, for instance, have taken a different tax approach, but it did not. It could, for instance, have told the Canadian public that the royalties which are paid in this country today exceed $1,498 million, while the royalties paid five years ago were only $235.2 million.
One could go on and read a great many figures and bore hon. members and anybody else who might wish to look at this report and the statistics, but let us not do that. Let us simply say that every indicator of consumption, of anticipated demand, of movement of exploration, seismic and drilling equipment, operations both offshore and onshore, in the past three years should have shown the government that if we were not to find ourselves in two positions of almost equal catastrophe-one being energy shortage and the other the imbalance of international payments-it should have done something to make us self-sufficient long ago, or promised self-sufficiency in the not too distant future. That did not happen.
While all these things were going on, the Government of Canada sought out scapegoats: it sought out the international consortium, it sought out anybody who made a profit, it sought out the consumer, and it sought out the

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
distributor. It attacked everybody from the little guy who puts gas in your tank to the big guy who takes it out of the ground. Everybody except the government was wrong; everybody else was to blame.
I submit that this has been rape by the government, by design and by the change of philosophy of the Government of Canada under the Liberal Party. It has been application of the philosophy that no one but the government is capable of doing the things Canadians need. I do not believe the voting public of Canada recognized this very slow and subtle philosophical change in the Liberal Party. It has had a reputation in the past of being reasonably alert to the needs of the Canadian people, but at this moment in time it is serving the political philosophies of those in cabinet and ignoring the actual needs of Canadians.
I do not buy all the objections that have been raised by various parties in this House in respect of the big corporations, because the Government of Canada has been able to control the ways and means of making sure it knows where every cent of profit in every company in this country has gone. The government has the ways and means to inflict government regulation or taxation upon those companies if they do not conduct themselves in a fashion which could be termed in the best interests of Canada. So all the taxes imposed on the companies do not get you anywhere except out of oil production.
I am just wondering, as I look at Bill C-8, how this policy is going to be structured and how we are going to get the various people in place. How are we going to gather up the expertise? The companies which have developed over the years have tried and proven employees, people who have shown the capacity to recognize formations where these resources exist. They would not be in the employ of these companies if they did not have that capacity. Where are we going to get the people who are needed with the proper expertise?
We do not have to look very far to see the progress of various business operations as they have taken place to know that expertise is something that is developed over a period of years; it is not something you can legislate or create as a business operation. Surely existing Crown corporations have proven this. Surely the method of appointment to positions of responsibility within these Crown corporations has proven beyond question that there is little hope for the success of Petro-Can if it is to be staffed by the same method. Surely it has been proven that the Government of Canada has never had the capacity to select people of this kind to conduct business in the private sector.
What is even worse about this situation is that the Goliath of government may very well, by its presence in legislation, further inhibit and deter the wish of companies presently in business to take the required action to fill the gap that will necessarily be here until such time as Petro-Can becomes the company which the government foresees. I am as concerned about the socialistic nature of the bill as I am about the lag in time when there will be no motivation for anybody else to develop and no capacity for the government to develop in the next ten years. This is a very serious factor which must be taken into consideration.

Had the government chosen to outline to the people of Canada the fact that there are certain aspects of the industry that need help, if the Government of Canada had said in sincerity that it would like to see these aspects owned and developed by Canadians, and if the Government of Canada had followed such a statement by making funds available to presently owned Canadian companies to go forward with this development, even though there might be risk to the taxpayer, there might be some justification for the government's move. If this had been the ways and means adopted to combat these scapegoats on whom the government has been putting the blame for the last five years, then perhaps there would be that justification. The fact is that small though some of these Canadian companies are, they do have the expertise which the Canadian government cannot get overnight and which it needs if this bill is to do what it says it will do. This would have been a reasonable substitute for what we have now.
The government has used a very poor policy in respect of the ownership of our resources because after years of knowledge of the ownership no clear formula has been established by which any private entrepreneur, national or international, would be well advised to invest his capital because he would have no idea of precisely where he would stand. Even if it were on paper, in the present economic climate nobody would know what the government would do next year. There would be no way of knowing whether or not the government would decide to impose a further tax.
Certainly, when the government imposed an income tax on business structures in this country which reduced their profit to nil, or in some cases to less than nil, they were not putting forward policies which would encourage the development of our petroleum-based industries. They may wish to blame it on provinces, they may wish to blame it on luck or anything they like, but their own behaviour has been detrimental to the development of the supply of this vital product-and Bill C-8 will not correct this situation overnight.
As I said earlier, I am concerned about the method and the means of financing this organization. I recall very well the debates that took place in respect of the financing bill for Air Canada and CNR in the last parliament. There was no way in which the minister and the officials responsible were going to place before the committee of the House of Commons the necessary facts and figures to determine whether there was any business justification for some of the moves for which money was being borrowed. In spite of this, money was borrowed.
Will it be the same for Petro-Can? Will we find ourselves, as taxpayers, in an identical position? I wonder about this and I am concerned about it. Will the government, for instance, through its right to buy shares, be able to pour money through the back door of the company to the detriment of the private enterprise which might be left, and then put it in a competitive position in which it will be the sole operator? Is it the intention to nationalize the entire oil structure? I sometimes wonder if that is not precisely what it is, hidden though it may be. The sincerity of the government must be challenged, and it is high time they levelled with us. It is my feeling that there has

been blatant exploitation of the minds of millions of Canadians who have no way of knowing what is best for them except what they are told by their leaders.
I submit that the justification for the bill before us is a group of misleading statements intended to create a climate of political feeling which might make it possible for the government to pass Bill C-8 and thus socialize a large section of our economy. When we do that, we may very well find ourselves not only lacking money for the development of the company but lacking money to buy the oil we will need.
In the name of democracy, this is another step in the paralytic, socialistic program of the Trudeau administration. As usual, leadership, management and ingenuity, characteristic of our own development as a nation, are utterly lacking in the present government. I sincerely hope that some rules and regulations will be laid down and they will become a part of this act, so that we are not writing another blank cheque for a political party to appoint its defeated candidates to find oil for Canada for generations to come.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have before us Bill C-8 to establish a national petroleum company. I find it very interesting that no Liberal speakers other than the minister have risen to defend this bill. I think they are rather embarrassed by it. Also, of course, the Conservatives are criticizing it most vociferously, as is indicated by their "head in the sand" approach to the whole energy crisis in this country!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: It is not the head that is in the sand, but the oil.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
If you dig a little deeper you might find oil, fellows, but I do not think so. The point is that this bill has some potential, but knowing the Liberal cabinet and traditional Liberal governments, I am afraid it appears to be mere tokenism in solving the vast energy problems of this country. I was rather intrigued by the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) when he opened the debate on this bill and I would like to read what he said as reported in Hansard:
This bill is a most important element in the government's long-term planning to secure adequate supplies of energy to meet our national needs. It is firmly rooted in the basic objectives of our energy and resource policies which are to ensure for Canadians adequate and reliable supplies at reasonable prices, as well as a direct share in the wealth which development of our resources generates.
Isn't that interesting? There, in a nutshell, is supposed to be the national energy policy; that is to say, adequate and reliable supplies, reasonable prices, and a direct share in the wealth of our resources. I would like to analyse that statement of the minister, look at the so-called aims of the government and see whether they have been fulfilled at all or whether it is possible, under this government, to fulfil those three objectives.
The first thing the minister wants in a national energy policy is adequate and reliable supplies of oil. The first question is, adequate and reliable supplies for whom? I ask this question because if we look at the development of the oil industry in this country we see that because it is over 90 per cent owned by multinational, foreign oil companies, someone must benefit other than Canadians. The
Petro-Canada
past history of the development of our resources of oil is that we have exported over half our supplies to the United States because the oil industry in this country is American-controlled. As a result, today we have a crisis in supply.
If the minister is serious about the importance of having adequate and reliable supplies, a long time ago this government would have told the National Energy Board to do some independent analyses to determine the extent of our oil reserves, instead of taking the figures of the oil companies verbatim; because if the oil companies wanted to export oil, being foreign-owned it was to their advantage to keep telling this government and the National Energy Board that our oil supplies would last for tens and tens of years into the future, to the end of the decade and beyond. But we have found out very recently, through a new National Energy Board report with respect to which some independent analysis work was done, that Canada is facing an energy shortage with regard to oil: within two years we will begin to see problems of indigenous supply and by 1982 we will become a net importer of oil.
If there had been any seriousness about having an adequate and reliable supply, it seems to me a government such as the previous Liberal government or its Conservative predecessor would have asked the National Energy Board to undertake an independent analysis. It was not done and as a result we are now paying for that lack of foresight.
The New Democratic Party, in the twenty-ninth parliament, argued vigorously for something to be done to control the exports to the United States, and because we were in a minority parliament and had some power in terms of votes we were able to convince the government, although it wanted to continue these exports, to impose some export controls. I would remind the House that in 1972 we were exporting 1.1 million barrels a day and by 1973 we had increased the figure to 1.3 million barrels a day. At that time we were exhausting our chief, known conventional oil reserves in Alberta at a rate which was detrimental to this country, and we were able to pressure the government into cutting back on oil exports. This is now a belated and accepted policy to serve Canadian interests.
Because we are now running short of oil, we have to look for oil in more expensive areas, that is, from the Athabasca oil sands, the High Arctic or bringing in expensive synthetic oil. When we consider the past development of our oil supply system, we see that it has been primarily of advantage to the multinationals and their markets in the United States because they have been able to tap our cheap, known oil reserves. Now that we are running short we have to pay higher prices for our own oil because we have to get it from more expensive sources.
The interesting thing is that when we look at the multinational oil companies and their plans for future development of sources of oil in this country, they are still using the argument that to make the development of the oil sands, or the Arctic oil, profitable not only must they have a higher price but they must have the right to export that oil. They argue that to bring it from the Arctic, large volumes are needed to obtain economies of scale; the

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
market in western Canada is not large enough to absorb it, so the oil will have to be exported. Unless we reverse that kind of thinking we will be perpetuating the mistakes that we made back in the 1950s and 1960s by continuing to export a precious resource and not really thinking about the future needs of Canada. As long as the oil industry is 90 per cent foreign-controlled we will be up against this problem and we will not be able to ensure adequate and reliable supplies of oil.
On the first ground, the government has failed in its energy policy to ensure reliable supplies for Canada, and it will be touch and go in the years ahead to ensure an adequate supply. As I have maintained, if we do not regain some control over our oil industry we will still have to succumb to those arguments which put us into this predicament in the first place. The second part of the minister's national energy policy is said to give Canadians oil at reasonable prices. That is very interesting. Let me go back just briefly. In 1972, oil sold in this country at $2.80 a barrel. The price of oil imported into eastern Canada from Venezuela and the Middle East was about $2.50 a barrel. By 1973, as the world oil crisis began to develop, the companies in Canada were able to pressure the price of oil up from $2.80 to $3.80 a barrel. A year later, in 1974, it went up to $6.50 a barrel. In a month or so there will be another first ministers' energy conference and I predict that our oil, which is now priced at $6.50 a barrel, will soon be $8.50.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), in many statements keep referring to moving the Canadian price up to the world price which now ranges anywhere between $11 and $13 a barrel. Indeed, the commitment to the Syncrude project in the Athabasca oil sands already guarantees the world price for oil coming from Alberta. Studies show that this price will continue to escalate from about $13 a barrel at the time the plant comes into operation at the end of this decade up to an incredible figure of $35 a barrel in the year 2003.
Will we have reasonable prices under the energy policy of this government? I say no, because the interesting thing about the pricing which I have described for conventional crude is that the cost of production has not increased; indeed, for the conventional crude supplies coming out of the ground now in Alberta, the cost of production in some cases has declined. Companies were quite content with $2.80 a barrel in 1972; today they are receiving $6.50 and because of that consumers have to pay more. Every time one fills a home heating oil tank or drives up to a gas pump, the difference can be seen.
We often think of energy just in terms of heating a home or running a car. We must also remember that when energy prices increase, so do prices in all other areas of our economy. Farmers, who are consumers of the largest amounts of fuel, have to pay more to operate their combines and tractors, which means that food prices increase. If a manufacturing plant has to pay more for its energy supply, that extra cost is reflected in the cost of the manufactured product.
A policy of reasonable prices, as a goal of this government in terms of energy, has failed. I refer again to the previous parliament, when in the winter months of 1973 we were able to maintain a voluntary freeze on the price

of oil products in this country. The government would have been quite willing to take it off that January, but we said we would defeat them on the issue and go to the people and they backed down. We also pressed for an export tax so that the windfall gains resulting from the lower Canadian price would not go automatically to the oil companies when our oil was exported to the United States and Americans bought it at the world price. In that sense we gained a bit of an advantage, but now in this majority situation the government has full sway and they are allowing prices to increase.
As long as we have the situation where one half of the country is dependent on western oil, and the area east of the Ottawa Valley is dependent on oil from Venezuela and the Middle East-because we have no all-Canadian pipeline-we will be in a dilemma as to how to achieve a Canadian price at a level lower than the world price, a level related to cost or a level which, by consensus between government and industry, is to the advantage of Canada.
If we could have a two-price system for oil, and if we could keep the price of our oil below the exaggerated and artificial world level, it would be of advantage to our manufacturing industry wherein jobs are created and it would give industry some stimulus and advantage in world trade. But we cannot do that unless as part of this government's energy policy we have a pipeline to eastern Canada in order to get western Canadian oil to the east or, vice versa, offshore oil to the west.
The Sarnia to Montreal pipeline proposal is really laughable. The pipeline is not big enough to carry the volume of oil that is needed in the east or, if it is reversible, in the west. Another point is interesting, too, and I shall come back to it later. The oil industry is asking the government to subsidize operating costs. We are now at the point, because of lack of foresight and lack of policy, of allowing the oil industry in this country to be foreign-owned, where we are faced with paying higher and higher prices for oil. I say the government has failed on that point and I do not see anything in this bill or in the intentions of the government to stop this artificial escalation in oil prices.
The third part of the minister's energy policy which intrigues me is his aim to have the people of Canada own a direct share in the wealth of our energy resources. I assume that would come about through our tax policies and a fair economic rent on the oil that is in the country, and therefore it should benefit Canadians. Looking at the past policies of the government, I do not see how anyone in his right mind could say that we have had a direct and fair share in our resources. In 1969, 79 per cent of the mining industry and the owners of the oil and gas wells in this country paid no federal income tax whatsoever. To take it from the general to the particular, in the period 1965 to 1971 Imperial Oil, the Canadian subsidiary of the multinational Exxon, paid income tax at the rate of 19 per cent on net earnings of over $1.5 billion.
The Minister of Finance likes to bring forth the fact that corporations are taxed at a rate of around 50 per cent, but look at Imperial's rate of 19 per cent for those years: that was the tax rate, in that period, for a married man with a

wife and two children who earned only $11,000 a year. This is the government's idea of a fair share of the wealth of the oil industry. Another example in the years 1964 to 1969 is Shell Oil Company, also a subsidiary of an American parent. It had net earnings of over $516 million, and did not pay one penny in federal income tax. Not one cent of economic gain through taxes came to this government.
I have given examples of the tax policy of the middle 1960s and early 1970s. Since oil prices have escalated so dramatically in this country, we have a situation where oil companies are receiving record profits. One should read the financial pages to see the figures for the past two years. In the third quarter of 1974 the profits earned by Western Oils increased 103 per cent over the same period of 1973. Gulf Oil had an after-tax profit for 1969 of $45.5 million. In 1973 their profit jumped to $101.7 million, and in 1974 it increased to $161 million, a 60 per cent increase in one year. Nor can Imperial Oil cry poverty. In 1969 its after-tax profits were $96 million; by 1973 they were $228 million and, while we do not have the complete figures for 1974, in the first nine months of that year their profits were $252 million.
What kind of share of those revenues is the government getting through its tax system? I say, very little, in light of the tax concessions given to those companies. Prior to the 1974 budget an automatic depreciation allowance was given to the oil companies. They could deduct one-third of their production profits according to a depletion formula. That has now been changed to an earned depletion with a maximum of 25 per cent-a minor improvement, and rather negligible when you look at today's profit figures. Not only did they have a depreciation allowance in the past, but there was also a 100 per cent write-off of exploration and development costs. This has now been reduced to 30 per cent. It always amuses me to see the advertisements on television in which the oil companies tell the Canadian public how expensive it is to find oil. They do not tell the other side of the story, that all that expense, up to the last budget, could be written off for tax purposes.
The share of the profits from the oil that belongs to the people of Canada has not been accruing to the people, through the tax policy of this government, nor is it likely to do so in the years ahead. Through concessions, Canada has given all kinds of capital to oil companies and in return we have been paying higher and higher prices for oil. The minister says we should be getting a share of the earnings of these multinationals-Gulf, Shell, Imperial, Texaco, etc.-but if he and the government had been serious we would have seen a change in the budget. The concessions in the budget are still there to a large degree.
The other point that we must always come back to is this: because over 90 per cent of the oil industry is foreign-owned, the money this government does not tax does not necessarily stay in the country to benefit Canadians. We find that the outflow of dividends from the subsidiaries in Canada to American multinational oil companies amounts to over 18 per cent. We are often told that the advantage of multinationals is that in return they can provide capital for Canadian subsidiaries to develop resources.
During the 1960s, the amount of capital inflow to the oil companies was only 17 per cent. They are sending out 18 per cent, or more than they are getting through capital
Petro-Canada
inflow. When you analyse the tax concessions in percentage terms for the past decade or so, you find we are paying out about 38 per cent of the capital of the oil companies. Not only do we give them money through tax concessions, but they come to the government for direct grants. Imperial Oil is in the process of building a fertilizer plant at Redwater, Alberta, which was designed by a California company. The plant is not being built by Canadians but by engineers from the California construction company. To boot, by building a fence down the middle of the site of the fertilizer plant, Imperial Oil was able to get two DREE grants from this government amounting to some $10 million. Not only do these poor oil companies which are making so little money get tax concessions, but they get direct government grants as well. However, the minister still says we are benefiting from the economic grant of our resources.
Syncrude is another example of the kind of bad deal this government has perpetrated. However, I have dealt with this matter in other speeches and I will let it go for now. If we really want a national oil company to fulfil the aims of the minister, namely, to have an adequate supply at a reasonable price for Canadians and a reasonable share of the wealth of our oil industry, then in light of past exploitation through allowing the industry to be in the hands of another country, and the present energy crisis in terms of supply and price, the logical step is to have public ownership and control of the oil industry in Canada.
If we follow the pattern of the fifties and the sixties, what arguments can my friends in the Conservative Party, or anyone else, put forward to say that that kind of mistake will not be repeated in years to come? The pattern is there. The crisis is here, now, because of that pattern. However, we still hear arguments that we must leave the industry entirely in the control of the multinational oil companies. If that is the problem, we must find a solution, and the solution is public ownership and control. We should look at oil as we look at electricity. The oil industry should be a public utility, run by the people of Canada through a publicly-owned corporation, for the benefit of Canadians.
I now come to the bill. The Liberal government has belatedly put before the House this bill to establish a national petroleum company. A crisis had to develop before they recognized the necessity of the Canadian people, through their government, having some control over the industry. When you look at the bill in print, you see it has sweeping terms of reference and wide powers. In my short experience in this House I have learned not to trust what is down in black and white but to examine the philosophy and intent of the government of the day. When I see the Minister of Finance listen to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and then start qualifying the degree of involvement that this national petroleum company will have in the whole oil industry, I conclude it will be totally inadequate: it will be mere tokenism as long as we have a Liberal government trying to administer it. In my opinion, this is an attempt belatedly to recognize the fact that we need some public control. However, there is fear on the part of the government to seize the bull by the
4208

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
horns and take direct and positive action; this is the problem.
What are the plans of the Liberal government for this national petroleum company? I do not want to sound as though I am predicting. I hope I am wrong when I say that the same thing will happen as has happened with the transportation industry in this country; this government will end up subsidizing the oil companies in unprofitable areas. Just as our existing Crown corporations run by Liberals tend to subsidize the private sector by taking over and operating the inefficient areas, the multinationals will require the national petroleum company to do the same. The national petroleum company will be given the task of exploring in less promising areas. It will only have minority involvement or control in some of the major energy developments in this country. I therefore conclude it will not fulfil its real purpose. It will be mere windowdressing by only being involved in some insignificant joint ventures, leaving the multinational oil companies firmly in control of policy related to supply and price.
A more positive step by this government would be to use the national petroleum company to take over the largest company in this country, Imperial Oil, and use that company as a pace-setter or model for the rest of the country. In other words, through Imperial Oil we would be able to set prices, exploration policy and energy development generally. With that kind of action the national petroleum company would really mean something. However, I very much doubt that the government will move in that direction. It would be a splendid opportunity for Canada and future Canadians to regain control of our resources; we would be able to set prices, control supplies and hire Canadians to develop those resources.
We have the ability in this country; we have modern support industries which could build the components for any energy development; we have engineers and technologists who have graduated from our universities, and we have the financing available. The only people left with any great inferiority complex are the members of the Liberal and Conservative parties who always say we cannot do this by ourselves, we need the multinationals to do it for us. Surely we can learn from our mistakes of the past, namely, allowing the multinationals to exploit our national resources.
I appeal to the silent Liberal backbenchers to stand up and argue before the minister and the House that we need a national petroleum company with some power and not mere tokenism. To fail to move in the direction of public ownership of our resource industries will perpetuate the sell-out of our national resources. To fail to act meaningfully, positively and vigorously by means of public ownership at this time will result in future generations cursing us for our short-sightedness. This is not the time for half-measures; it is the time for full public control and ownership of our energy resources.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to say a few words on this bill which establishes Petro-Canada. I have noted the rather grudging support of the NDP for a national
[Mr. Symes.l
petroleum corporation. I am somewhat disappointed at the calibre of the opposition offered by the Conservative Party with regard to Bill C-8 which proposes to establish a national petroleum corporation. When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) submitted this bill for second reading last Tuesday and articulated the rationale for a national petroleum corporation, we honestly expected opposition to this matter to be based on substance or the approach of the bill, rather than the time-worn and outmoded argument that private enterprise is being undermined. This is what the PCs seem to be promoting. I think the stage has been reached at which members of the Conservative Party should accept the fact that private enterprise, for all its dynamism and strategic role in Canada's economy, cannot meet all the demands imposed on it.
Bill C-8 represents a bold and constructive effort by this government to secure adequate supplies of energy to meet our long-term national needs. As spelled out by the minister last week, the basic objectives of our energy and resource policies are designed to ensure adequate and reliable supplies at reasonable prices and to acquire a direct share in the wealth which development of our resources generates. We cannot allow ourselves to become embedded in an ideological quagmire that will ultimately sink us into economic disaster. Instead, we must recognize that the role of government is going to increase steadily in areas where the private sector is unable to satisfactorily meet all requirements.
The government has always recognized the vital role of private enterprise in the growth and development of this country and it has no intention of curtailing its continued participation in Canada's future. But the complexities of international trade and the gigantic appetite for energy generated by sophisticated industrial societies dictate greater supervision and control of our economies than can be achieved by a laissez-faire approach.
The decision to propose legislation to establish a national petroleum company was taken only after an extensive and thorough examination of Canada's long-term energy needs. There is no point in trying to devise instant remedies for problems after they arise if we can avoid such pitfalls by taking sound and far sighted initiative which will ensure a steady supply of energy on a long-term basis. To be confident of adequate supplies we need to know as much as possible about the extent and mix of energy resources available in Canada. We have reason to believe that Canada is generously endowed with several energy products-oil, natural gas, uranium and coal. However, our present knowledge as to the extent of Canadian resources of these commodities is limited. In addition, the costs associated with finding and producing these resources cannot be known until they have been located. Some will be in the remote locations of the Canadian north or in underwater locations; others, such as the oil sands of Alberta or the heavy oils of Saskatchewan and Alberta, require the development of new technology to permit extraction of the larger potentials of these resources.
Success in finding large amounts of oil, gas and uranium will permit Canadians to have confidence in the security
March 18, 1975

of their energy supplies and permit the holding of a level of resources adequate to ensure long-term Canadian needs. The government has taken numerous steps over the years to encourage exploration for these reasons. The investment climate in the industry was supported by our national oil policy ensuring the opportunity to sell Canadian output in Canadian markets. Tax or royalty policies have been framed with the objective of balancing investment incentives and a sharing of the profits of the sale of these resources.
The government has, in recent years, prohibited increased export commitments in natural gas and has limited the export of oil and petroleum products to ensure adequate supplies for Canadian needs. The government has recently indicated its intention to see to the building of a pipeline to Montreal to carry Canadian crude oil to this market which currently depends virtually entirely on imported petroleum.
The federal government has also made numerous investments in energy industries. Eldorado Nuclear Ltd. has explored for uranium; Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. has developed a successful technology for nuclear electricity generation; Panarctic Oils Ltd. has explored for oil and gas in the Arctic Islands in a joint venture between the Government of Canada and several private firms. These, along with the recently announced Syncrude project, are the most prominent examples of federal investments to develop energy capacity for Canadians.
A large amount of money is needed to carry out further exploration. This work must be done over the coming few tears to locate additional reserves to be made available to the market as the presently known reserves begin to fall short of Canadian needs. The territory which is regarded as promising is vast. The task is a large one. Canadian petroleum resources are known to include a vast potential in the oil sands and heavy oils. There remain, however, significant technological advances to be achieved if the largest portion of these resources is to be extracted.
The government is anxious to ensure that exploration and research activities are undertaken in the expectation that they will yield quantities of oil and gas which are comfortably sufficient for projected Canadian needs over the short and long term. If the resource base proves to be large, it would be our aim to develop as much of these assets as is compatible with our goals for industrial development, employment and high income levels as well as those of security of supply, regional development and environmental protection.
The present prospects for substantial reserves being found are high. The results of drillings to date in the north and of other geological and geophysical work are promising, particularly with respect to natural gas. Similarly, eastern offshore exploratory work has located some gas but not yet in commercially viable quantities. The exploratory work is dependent on the investment decisions of private firms in the industry. These firms quite properly look to the immediate production of resources they discover in order to realize returns on their investment. The holding of significant reserves which would provide a longer period of protection for projected Canadian needs is more properly a public responsibility.
Petro-Canada
The national petroleum company will be empowered to undertake some exploration in Canadian frontier regions and to participate in the funding of research into oil sands and heavy oil production. This company will also be available to stimulate further exploration in the frontier regions. The large job of satisfactorily exploring these areas can be accelerated by the participation of this agency of government. The fuller information on Canadian energy resources and their costs which this should provide will make easier the task of formulating public policy in energy. With this information we will be able to decide more confidently on the acceptable rate of production. The government will be able to avoid an unreasonable increase in prices dictated by a few producing countries prepared to make political use of their oil production. In addition, to its own activities and success, this company will receive for the Canadian public a share of the wealth created by these resources.
In its exploration activities, the corporation will seek to stimulate activity by entering into joint ventures with private firms or by entering into other relationships appropriate to this industry. In this way, smaller Canadian ventures which currently find it difficult to sustain the costly and lengthy exploration effort will be able to participate with others and with a national petroleum company in this work.
In view of the significance which new technological developments in oil sands and heavy oils would have for petroleum supply in Canada, the government is prepared to share the financial burden of this research and development. With respect to the oil sands, this research and development will be undertaken co-operatively with the province of Alberta and those companies in the private sector which have an interest in such work. Federal participation will be accomplished through the national petroleum company so that it can participate in the making of new technology available with benefits for Canadians.
Research is also called for in the development of a capability to extract heavy oils from the deposits in Alberta and Saskatchewan. In addition, the government would want to encourage other promising research into fuels technology. The national petroleum company could stimulate, support and participate in such research.
The government looks to this corporation to help contribute to an increased Canadian presence in the petroleum exploration business. Foreign investment in this effort has not been and will not be refused where it is compatible with Canadian interests. Nevertheless, Canada has the financial and other resources to play a more significant role in the exploration for and development of its petroleum resources. This corporation could add to the Canadian presence by its operations and could seek to operate jointly with Canadian and foreign firms undertaking exploratory activity in Canada.
The exploration and research roles of the national petroleum company would, therefore, have several objectives; first, to advance the definition of the Canadian energy resource base; second, to hold reserves adequate to ensure Canadian security of supply; third, to stimulate the
28996-61%

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
private sector to further exploration and research work by means of joint ventures; fourth, to permit energy policies to be formulated with fuller knowledge of the volume and cost of Canadian energy resources; fifth, to achieve a greater Canadian presence and acquire a share of the wealth accruing to investors in the petroleum industry; and sixth, to help stimulate improved technology in the production and use of energy from whatever sources are most appropriate.
I should make clear that commitments of this sort are not free from risk. We do, however, have confidence in the Canadian resource potential, and Petro-Canada will be an important instrument in its development. I should also point out that results cannot be expected overnight. This marks the beginning of what will inevitably be a long road marked by successes and disappointments, but contributing in the end to both Canadian income and security of supply.
In this general task of exploration and research for the identification of Canadian energy reserves there is considerable opportunity for all those interested to play a part. The area is vast, the demand for petroleum is large and increasing, and Canadian policy supports balanced development under appropriate safeguards of Canadian interests. The national petroleum company will contribute, along with the present and future investors, to these developments.
Turning now from the development of Canadian resources, an important role may develop for the national petroleum company in the importing of foreign petroleum. While steps are being taken to move Canadian crude to Montreal to supply some of this market, we will continue to look to foreign production to fill a portion of our national petroleum needs. It is, therefore, of considerable importance that all possible steps be taken to achieve the greatest possible security of those imported supplies.
The government may be able to play an important role in purchasing petroleum and petroleum products from foreign markets. The international petroleum markets have been changing and foreign supplies are increasingly in the hands of the governments of producing countries. It is the government's intention to equip itself to deal with these and other suppliers where they are able to provide secure supplies for Canadian needs. The national petroleum company will, if the need arises, operate in international markets as a purchaser of petroleum.
The federal government has long been active in energy industries. The government currently owns an uranium exploration company, Eldorado Nuclear Ltd., an uranium holding company, Uranium Canada Ltd., a 45 per cent interest in a company engaged in exploration in the Arctic Islands, Panarctic Oils Ltd., and a coal deposit in British Columbia, namely, Dominion Coal block which accounts for something like 10 per cent of Canada's entire reserves of coal. These ventures all involve raw materials which are used to produce energy.
Energy sources are interchangeable in many uses. Homes can be heated, for example, by energy in the form of electricity, oil, gas or coal. Electricity can be generated from water power or from oil, gas or coal-fueled turbines. Nuclear reactors using uranium in the Canadian developed CANDU process have proven highly successful in the

generation of electricity. This interchangeability will be effected over time by new technological developments and by the costs involved in using one or other of these energy sources in different applications.
Whether under public or private direction, a significant part of Canadian economic activity is located in energy-producing activities. The largest part of this production is vital to other Canadian industrial activities and to the support of the Canadian lifestyle. With its rigorous climate, vast geography and traditionally high living standards, Canada takes a special economic interest in its energy sector. The government has always recognized the special status of this industry. The creation of the national petroleum company will add to the instruments available to the Government of Canada to advance Canadian interests in secure and adequate energy supplies and in the sharing of the wealth which Canadian resource endowments make possible.
I am certainly pleased that this bill has been endorsed by some members of the opposition. I think it is reasonable to expect that the rest of the opposition will recognize the need for this kind of legislation so that the government can better promote long-term energy supplies for the benefit of all Canadians.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the primary objective of Bill C-8 is to establish a Crown-owned petroleum company within the petroleum industry. In this bill, Petro-Canada is given the authority to explore, develop and exploit hydrocarbon deposits within and without Canada; to carry out research and development projects related to hydrocarbons in other fields; to engage in exploration, production, distribution, refining and marketing of fuel; and, finally, to negotiate for and acquire petroleum products from abroad.
In other words, this bill will give this Crown corporation authority to do everything and anything related to the petroleum industry, from filling gas tanks, changing tires, to running seismic surveys in the South China Sea. No government agency should be given this kind of authority to waste the taxpayers' money; we would be shirking our responsibility if we permitted them to do so. We in this party are opposed to this concept. We are opposed to the establishment of Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation with authority granted to it by this bill. We are opposed for a great number of reasons, but five of the major ones are: first, and probably most important, it simply is not needed; second it is going to be very costly to the taxpayers of Canada, and Lord knows, when filling out income tax returns at this time of year all taxpayers become aware that they are already overtaxed. We need less calls upon our money, not more, and this particular call will be virtually a money sump in terms of expenditure of taxpayers' dollars.
The third reason is that it could, and likely will, be harmful to the existing industry, and rather than aiding our supply situation will in fact exacerbate it, resulting in diminished security of supply for Canadians instead of enhanced security of supply. The fourth reason is that it will deflect public and official attention away from what is the major and significant problem in energy supply in this country, namely, the total lack of a national energy policy. The government's remedy of creating a Crown
March 18, 1975

corporation so that it will not have to bother addressing itself to this problem or to finding solutions is totally unsatisfactory.
The fifth reason is simply that there are better ways of accomplishing all of the intended goals of Petro-Canada, and indeed of lot of other goals that are not set out as intended goals for Petro-Canada but which should be the intended goals of a rational, national energy policy.
As to the question of whether a national petroleum company is needed, one really need look no further than the government's own document to which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) referred last Wednesday when speaking on second reading of this bill. He claimed it was published by himself, and I suppose it was, in July, 1973. It contains an extensive discussion of the pros and cons of a national petroleum company in pages 186 to 191 inclusive.
In his comments on this document last Wednesday during the discussion on a national petroleum company, the minister indicated that the arguments pro and con roughly balanced out. That is hogwash. They balance out numerically only in that there are ten reasons for, and nine against. If one looks at the document, examines it and reads the arguments with the least bit of objectivity, he cannot help but reach the conclusion that a national petroleum company is not needed nor is it desirable.
The minister indicated in his remarks that although this report did not in fact come out in favour of a national petroleum company, events subsequent to its publication have caused him to change his mind. I would ask, how much subsequent to that does he mean? In a speech on October 25, 1973, about four months after this document was published, the minister more or less indicated to the House that he had decided in favour of a national petroleum company. One cannot help but reach the conclusion that the minister decided for his own reasons, philosophical or whatever, that a national petroleum company was to be created. He decided he was going to build this empire as one of his accomplishments, perhaps with which to launch his leadership bid upon the retirement of the present leader of the Liberal Party. Who knows why he wanted to create this empire? The fact is that his own document, which I commend to him for reading, states that there is no reason for a national petroleum company because it is not needed.

You had better read Pierre Berton's book. Does Air Canada fill us full of pride? Every experienced traveller that I know of tries to fly CP. Let us consider that successful Crown corporation, Polymer. The most successful part of its operations are international, with headquarters in Belgium. This Crown corporation has its international headquarters in Belgium because it finds the tax and fiscal regime in Canada oppressive. Compare Polymer with CIL an other Canadian company of roughly the same size in terms of capitalization, to see which one out-performs the other.
The Canada Development Corporation is another great Crown corporation that will fill us all full of pride. It recently moved its headquarters to The Netherlands because it could not operate under Canada's tax and fiscal regime. This would be almost laughable if it were not so sad and did not cost Canadian taxpayers so much in terms of money and pride. Anybody who looks at it must feel a little sick to realize that a Crown corporation like the Canada Development Corporation must move to The Netherlands to find a tax regime which will allow it to operate at a profit. This is incredible.
The second reason given in this document for establishing a national petroleum company is that there is a need to increase the level of knowledge of all phases of the operation of the petroleum industry. Whose level of knowledge does that speak of? Clearly, it is the government's. I cannot argue with the suggestion that the government's level of knowledge is insufficient, because that has been amply demonstrated to us. What this amounts to is an admission of incompetence.
With the many hundreds, even thousands of advisers in this huge pyramid behind the minister, they come out with the admission that they really do not have any knowledge of the oil industry. Is this the only way they can gain knowledge, by going into the oil business? As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said at one time in the House, and I paraphrase him, he had never laid an egg but he did not have to be a hen to know how to make an omelette. He said that in reply to the challenge that he had no knowledge about a subject, and his reply is precisely applicable in this situation.
If the government lacks knowledge, then, for goodness sake, it should fire the individuals who are currently responsible for gathering that knowledge, because there is no reason for them to lack knowledge about any aspect of the oil industry. It is one of the most regulated industries

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
in the world. Companies cannot get permits without applications to the National Energy Board. That board is constantly holding hearings on one subject or another. The industry is regulated in terms of exports. It is not allowed to drill without provincial permits. There is virtually no aspect of the industry that companies are allowed to engage in without getting a permit of one kind or another. Surely this provides the government with all the knowledge it needs.
If there is any truth in the suggestion that the government can get the necessary knowledge by going into the oil industry, then I would point out that the government has been running the Post Office for a good many years so why in the heck does it not have the knowledge to run it properly? Senator Manning, in a speech in Calgary last Wednesday, stated that any group of oil men in Calgary forgot more between supper and breakfast about the industry than any equivalent number of bureaucrats here in Ottawa would ever learn.
The third reason given in this document is that a national petroleum company could play a role in determining the criteria on which the government might base its policy regarding economic rent collection. Here, again, we have an admission of incompetence. This is an admission that in fact the finance department, in coming up with its scheme for taxation of the resource industry, did not know what it was doing: that is what this document says. They do not know how to collect an economic rent; that is patently obvious. We do not need this statement to know that; we need only look at what has happened to the oil and gas industry, the decrease in the amount of exploration and development that has taken place, and the decreasing supplies in proven, recoverable reserves to realize what serious damage has occurred as a result of the government's tax policies.
However, another aspect which worries me more than ignorance on the part of the government is that this is tantamount to stating that the government has adopted what amounts to a socialist philosophy. I hesitate to use that phrase because it sounds so noisy, so extreme. However, I have always been taught in school, and I still believe it, that the role of government is to fulfil certain expectations and certain obligations through its regulatory functions, its function of redistribution of income, and through a variety of activities which it is called upon to perform. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) called this civilization; I say it is the role of government.
The purpose of taxation is to provide funds to enable the government to fulfil these functions. That is why I and other Canadians pay taxes. We are contributing our bit to maintaining the government in the fulfilment of its roles and obligations. However, what this statement indicates is that in fact the government feels that the total income from the economy belongs to the central government, and that its role is simply to split up the income and then see how much will be left in the private sector. The government wishes to leave enough in the private sector and then find ways of spending what is left. This is a reversal of everything I have believed, have accepted, or have been taught.

I think we have reached a very sad state if in fact the philosophy of our government is that they own all the income and have first call on everything that an individual might earn or might gain as a result of his investment, and that we should be grateful for what is left in our hands. I cannot accept that philosophy.
The fourth argument is that a national petroleum company, if it controls sufficiently large volumes of petroleum reserves, will be able to exert an influence on the setting of crude oil and petroleum products' prices. That is a specious argument. The government has prices totally under control. What in the blazes is a national petroleum company going to do? Is it going to fight with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources about what the level should be? How can this sort of argument be put forward at the same time as a measure such as Bill C-32 is brought forward?
The fifth argument in the list of arguments in favour of the establishment of a national petroleum company is that such a company would encourage the upgrading and sale of refined products rather than crude oil. We have recently been told by the National Energy Board that very soon Canada will not have oil to sell in any form, crude or refined; indeed, we may not have enough oil with which to heat our homes. So that certainly is an invalid argument.
The sixth argument is that the major integrated oil companies carry out the bulk of their research in the country of their parent corporation, and that a national petroleum company would carry out its research in Canada. That is the first argument that makes some sense. But I hope the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources does not need reminding that we have the National Research Council, we have a research group in his department which used to be called the mines branch, we have a new energy institute funded by federal moneys in Alberta, we have the Alberta Research Council and the Saskatchewan Research Council, and we have the Petroleum Recovery Research Institute in Alberta. I have named just a few of the research institutes in Canada.
That there should be more money available for research in energy is self-evident, or should be to anybody who has paid attention to the recently published Science Council report. That cannot be argued. But that we need a national petroleum company to funnel the moneys into this research effort is an argument that does not stand up.
The seventh argument is that all aspects of the operations of a national petroleum company would be located in Canada and that we would derive certain benefits therefrom because other petroleum companies have branches of their operations in foreign companies. I do not know how the minister can ensure that the management of this company will have sufficient freedom to operate independently and still guarantee that they will stay in Canada. We have had the recent example, to which reference was made earlier, of another Crown corporation, the Canadian Development Corporation, which moved its headquarters to The Netherlands because it found that it was not profitable to operate in Canada. Is that not an indictment of this government's policies?
The eighth argument is that a national petroleum company would purchase more Canadian-produced goods than other petroleum companies. Again, if it is a commercial
March 18, 1975

enterprise it will purchase its supplies and goods on a normal commercial basis. If, in fact, the industrial situation, the tax situation and the fiscal situation in Canada are such that most companies go outside our borders to find their supplies, the solution lies in a change in the policies of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), and possibly of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), to stimulate demand.
The ninth argument is a beauty. It is that a national petroleum company would act to stimulate regional development in specific areas of the country. Can you see it doing so? Will our national petroleum company drill for oil somewhere where we need economic activity, instead of where geologists and geophysicists tell us it is to be found? The definition of the drilling program will be to look for oil where there is a weak Liberal candidate running and to drill a well in his constituency. It is patently absurd to suggest that any oil company will establish a drilling program on the basis of regional development. However, this is not the first absurd notion we have had from this government.
The tenth argument is that a national petroleum company could play an active role in government relations with other state-owned oil companies from which we import oil. Granted, this could be a role played by the corporation, but we already have a whole spate of Crown corporations which could play that commercial role. Now that the Minister of Supply and Services has some experience in buying oil, perhaps we can go to him.
These are the ten arguments on why we should establish a national petroleum company. Two of them hold a little water, eight are patently absurd and two or three are downright laughable. On the other side, eight arguments are put forward on why the establishment of a national petroleum company at this time is not a good idea. What are the eight arguments? The first argument is that it will cost a lot of money. Darn right it will cost a lot of money! This document estimates that $3 billion to $6 billion will be needed to develop the corporation to a state where it is a significant unit within the oil industry. That is a very conservative estimate. A reasonable estimate of how much of the taxpayers' money will be used before this Crown corporation can reach the stage where it can become a significant factor in the oil industry would be closer to $50 billion.
It is downright irresponsible for any member of this House to give a government agency the authority to spend that amount of our money in an activity about which it knows very little, has demonstrated considerable incompetence, and in an activity for which it is not necessary to have government directly involved.
The second item in this document points out quite clearly that this would be a bad investment and that we will likely get little or nothing back on our money when it is spent. The third item admits that it will be very difficult for a Crown corporation to compete with the private companies. That is a fact. The Crown corporation, without special privileges which will cost us money, cannot com-
Petro-Canada
pete with the private sector in this high-risk industry. The fourth item acknowledges the point I raised earlier, that in fact a national petroleum company could be detrimental to the existing oil and gas industry, thereby jeopardizing Canada's security of supply and thereby putting our future and our children's future in danger.
The fifth item is an acknowledgement of what I have just repeated. There is no way a Crown corporation can be as efficient as existing companies. Why should a Crown corporation engage in an activity in which it will be less efficient than companies currently operating? The sixth item is again an acknowledgement that the private sector in Canada is doing a very good job. The minister admits that. If the private sector is doing a good job, why try to drive it out of business? If the private sector is doing a good job why come in with some government colossus which will make it more difficult for the private sector to operate, and which will take large amounts of our money? Unless the government is philosophically committed, as are my colleagues to the left, to the state running everything, why do it? There cannot be any reason.
If the government is philosophically committed to socialism, that is fine, but we are looking for rational reasons. I think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is philosophically committed to the state running resource industries, and any members on the benches behind the minister who are deluding themselves with the feeling that they are members of a party which has confidence in the people of Canada, and confidence in the private sector, are in for a fall. If they repeat that nonsense to their constituents, they are also deluding their constituents.
The seventh item points out that we already have a number of regulatory bodies in connection with the energy industries, and that there is bound to be a conflict of interest at some time between the National Energy Board and the national petroleum company. This clearly cannot be in the best interests of Canada.
The eighth item is an admission that this question of chauvinistic pride or xenophobia, which will make us get behind it and really drive this national petroleum company to the front, does not exist because Canadians are just not chauvinistic, they are just not xenophobic, and they will not respond to that kind of rallying cry.
