How is there any improvement in toto if the Crown corporation robs other sectors of the industry of their equipment?
There are personnel limitations. If the national petroleum company hires expert personnel currently working for the other companies, then those people are no longer available to those companies. In toto how is the country benefitting?
There are capital limitations. What percentage of our gross national product will be allocated to the search for oil and gas? Whatever is taken by the national petroleum company will not be available to the private sector. Things will not be improved one iota, unless the government takes the taxes which it might spend on things like old age pensions and invests them in the oil and gas industry. If the government feels it is more important to build this huge colossus than to try to help Canadians, there is not much we can do but try to convince it otherwise.
It is difficult to reach any conclusion other than that a national petroleum company is going to diminish the amount of oil and gas available for Canadians, is going to diminish our security of supply, is going to diminish our ability to export, is going to increase our dependency on the Middle East and Venezuela, is going to make us more susceptible to pressures from overseas and will damage the economy rather than help it.
The fourth point, Mr. Speaker, and the main reason why we in this party oppose this move, is that it is going to deflect government, public, and private attention away from the need for a national petroleum policy. Such a policy was promised at least five years ago but has never
[Mr. Paproski.l
been produced. There has been an excellent analysis of the situation which has the makings of a policy if the government would only produce it. Instead it is trying to deflect attention from the lack of policy by creating this agency.
We must have a policy in order to encourage exploration and development, a policy that will enable companies and investors to construct and operate more tar sands plants. We need a policy that will encourage the upgrading of hydrocarbons to higher grades of fuel, plastics and fertilizers so that we can export a high value product rather than a low value product.
We need a national energy policy that will encourage research and development to find alternate forms of energy. The recently published report of the Science Council of Canada covered that subject fairly well. Regardless of how successful we are in exploiting hydrocarbon reserves, however, the fact of the matter is that they are finite. Eventually we will run out of hydrocarbons, gas and oil, so we have to find alternate sources. The research must begin now and we need a policy to encourage it. It is not good enough to say that we are going to create a Crown corporation to look after the problem. We need a policy that will encourage Canadian ownership of this important industry-not state ownership but Canadian ownership.
The government has no confidence in the people of Canada and does not think that they have enough faith in the country to invest in it. It believes that the little discretionary income we have to invest we would spend frivolously, and therefore it is not going to leave us that discretionary income but will tax it away. That is typical of the government. Virtually every problem in public policy has exactly the same solution, a new agency, a new Crown corporation, a new board-the Food Prices Review Board, the Foreign Take-over Review Board, the national petroleum company-every problem has the same solution. A computer could be programmed to develop that sort of policy, hire a new bunch of people, whatever the problem, create a new agency, give them the problem and then not worry about it any more. The phone book is full of these agencies.
I recently read an article that said there are 60,000 agencies in Italy. One day a man approached one of them in the afternoon looking for somebody. There was only one person there so he asked, "Doesn't anybody work here?" The reply was "In the morning they don't work; in the afternoon they don't come." We are approaching that situation in Canada-no matter what the problem, the solution is to create another agency. Mr. Speaker, even the Liberal Party is going to run out of defeated candidates to staff these agencies.
There is a complete lack of faith in Canadians and their willingness to participate in the growth of this country, or to get together and use their resources to invest in the country and help it reach the levels of which it is capable.
The fifth point is that there is a better alternative. Consider the question of Canadian ownership. On several occasions I have talked about the principal business test in the Income Tax Act which, more than any other aspect of legislation in this country, is responsible for our industries being as foreign-controlled as they are. That one aspect of the Income Tax Act means that it is cheaper for a foreign-
March 18, 1975

er to drill a well in Canada than it is for a Canadian. That just boggles the mind, Mr. Speaker. I cannot understand how we in Canada can tolerate a situation where a foreigner can invest in this country more cheaply than a Canadian can. Of course that is why the industry is foreign-owned.
It is easier to set up headquarters in the Netherlands and operate from there, but some of us want to stay in Canada and invest here in order that the country may grow. Mr. Speaker, we demand that the government give us this opportunity and stop creating these new agencies and Crown corporations that continually oppress us. Just give us the opportunity. On that happy note, Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-8, to establish a national petroleum company, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to give my support to this bill to establish a national petroleum company. The federal government is in a unique situation when compared with private concerns for setting up large scale operations of this nature. The time span between the period of initiation and the full-scale production stage can be appreciably reduced when a venture is backed by the resources of the government.
I very much wish to see the development in Canada of world-scale sized plants producing highly refined petroleum derivatives for international consumption. It is essential that these plants be owned or controlled by Canadians, and it is in this area that the federal government can and should become involved. I am not promoting public ownership of our major industries. I have always been a strong supporter of private enterprise, and I believe that this system makes for greater efficiency. We are presently, however, in a situation where venture capital is not easily obtainable for the purpose of setting up large scale undertakings in the field of energy resources. The development of potential sources of energy is of benefit to all Canadians, and the federal government is fully justified in becoming involved in this area.
I would like at some time in the future to see the gradual movement of Petro-Canada from the public to the private sector of our economy, perhaps through a vehicle

such as the Canada Development Corporation. However, until the company becomes firmly established it is necessary that it be operated as a Crown corporation.
This formula has worked successfully in the past. I would draw the attention of the House in particular to Polysar, a company established by the government in 1942 as Polymer Corporation Limited. What began as an emergency wartime operation has grown to become a major competitor in the international synthetic rubber market. Over the years Polysar has developed diversified interests throughout the world.
Since its take-over by the Canada Development Corporation in 1972. Polysar has continued to expand its range of activities, including the attainment of a 60 per cent interest in Petrosar, a world-scale petro-chemical plant currently being constructed near Sarnia, Ontario. This plant, which will produce one billion pounds of ethylene per year, as well as other related products, will be able to compete successfully with similar companies particularly in the United States, because of the economies of scale inherent in the operation. For the first time in Canada, ethylene will be available to us at a price as cheap as, or cheaper than, that available in the Gulf area of the United States. The success enjoyed by Polysar is an excellent indication of the possibilities which exist for similar success for Petro-Canada as a government-supported company.
An assured supply of energy is vital to Canada. There must exist an organization that is willing to gamble in order to make certain that our long and short term energy requirements are met. Petro-Canada will be in a position to take calculated risks with that end in mind. Participation in such projects as Syncrude and Panarctic Oils exemplifies this type of activity. The potential in these areas is enormous but the uncertainties involved make them unpopular areas of investment for private industry.
The terms of reference under which the company will operate are sufficiently broad to allow it to engage in operations involving all other forms of energy. Petro-Canada will therefore be able to act quickly to take advantage of opportunities as they present themselves.
As conventional fuel supplies are depleted, resource development will become increasingly more costly. A nationally owned petroleum company would be able to undertake research and development programs involving risks and expenditures which would be prohibitive for private industry. I feel this is one of the greatest advantages to be gained by the establishment of Petro-Canada. The refining and marketing of oil and natural gas supplies will be a secondary and less urgent aspect of the company's operations. Before nuclear fusion capability is developed-hopefully by the end of this century-our dwindling petroleum supplies will be called upon to provide the bulk of our short and medium term energy. No time must be wasted in finding and developing new reserves of conventional fuels.
Energy self-sufficiency is a goal toward which we must strive. We cannot rely on private industry, with over 90 per cent of that involved in energy development presently foreign-owned or controlled, to attach more than a secondary importance to this goal. International oil supplies are
March 18, 1975

subject to the whims of foreign governments which may not always have Canada's best interests in mind.
Even while economical and easily recoverable fuel supplies remain, it is essential that the technology be developed now to ensure a continuing supply of energy from Canadian sources. The funding available to Petro-Canada will allow extensive research programs to be carried on. The success of Petro-Canada as a profit making company should be of secondary importance to the object of guaranteeing a continuous supply of energy for Canadians.
One of the most serious implications for Canada of the operation of foreign controlled oil companies in this country is the resultant lack of Canadian control over research and development in this industry. Canada has proportionately little industrial research and development activity, and this is the result of the involvement of foreign companies in Canadian industry. While it is true that Imperial Oil Limited, Gulf Oil Canada Limited and Shell Canada Limited all maintain substantial research and development operations, this activity is directed largely from the head offices of the foreign parent companies. There is no reason for a company such as Imperial Oil, the third largest industrial firm in Canada, with annual sales of approximately $2.5 billion, to be unable to establish a completely independent research and development facility.
Petro-Canada will enable us to achieve this significant goal of establishing Canadian control over a major research and development establishment within the petroleum industry.
While there are presently several options in the energy field which merit consideration, such as geothermal, tidal, wind and solar power, it is necessary that there be a commercial organization capable of translating these possibilities into practice. This is another area of which industrial research and development is an essential component. Over the long term, research should be undertaken into alternate energy forms to enable us to consider using our petroleum supplies solely for the production of plastics. Should the day arrive when we completely run out of hydrocarbons, a company such as Petro-Canada would not become obsolete, as it could modify its operations to enable it to produce the building blocks necessary for the production of plastics. All that would be required would be changing from hydrocarbons for the raw materials used, to carbon dioxide, one of the products of the combustion of hydrocarbons, which can be converted back to organic chemicals through the methanol synthesis process, as has been successfully done in the past. The only problem is one of economics, not technology.
Some hon. members may not be aware of the importance of the plastics industry in this country. We currently consume a greater volume of plastic each year than we do steel, and this industry can only continue to grow in importance.
It is also possible that Petro-Canada, as an able competitor in the petroleum industry, will be a leader in developing an attitude of responsible corporate citizenship among the oil companies. Either by example or through the realities demanded by competitive business practices, Petro-
Petro-Canada
Canada may make the petroleum industry more responsive to the needs of the Canadian people.
That, essentially, is what Petro-Canada is all about- making the oil and natural gas industries responsible to the Canadian people. What is needed is the development of long term goals and priorities in order to guarantee the development of an energy industry within Canada which will be immune to the uncertainties of the world situation.
A central element of the problem of short-term supply with relation to oil is the fact that we will, for some years to come, remain dependent on foreign suppliers for a percentage of our crude oil. Therefore it is important that we maintain a favourable position for negotiating with, in particular, the OPEC countries. There has been a growing reluctance on the part of these nations to deal with large, multinational oil companies, and a preference for dealing with nationally owned companies from various countries. As one of Petro-Canada's primary functions will be to obtain supplies of crude oil, international negotiations will, of necessity, be carried on by the company.
I am certain that the act to establish Petro-Canada will long be regarded as a landmark piece of legislation, one of which all Canadians should be proud. Energy production is of an importance second only to food production in this country, and it is heartening that the present intolerable situation which involves the foreign ownership of such a large percentage of our energy resources is at long last being, in some measure, rectified.
The question of foreign ownership has long been of concern to me, and I welcome this action as a positive example of government involvement in Canadian industry. I sincerely hope that this will be only a beginning and provide an impetus to projects designed to establish world scale sized plants in Canada for the production of high technology content commodities from our vast natural resources. Through action of this nature the government can give Canadian industry the push it needs to break further away from its role as a supplier of raw materials towards a position of being a major exporter of manufactured products.
In reply to those who feel that a nationally owned oil company could not compete successfully with private industry, I would draw their attention to the fact that, besides the United States, Canada is the only industrialized nation that does not have a national petroleum company. As an example of a successful company of this type one may consider the British Petroleum Company. Approximately 68 per cent of this company is owned by the British government. It has long been a highly successful competitor on the international scene, with diversified interests in many areas related to its primary object of developing and marketing petroleum supplies. It is involved in producing many high technology petroleum products, including several families of plastics.
It is too easy to criticize this bill on the grounds that it involves risks being taken with public money. We cannot afford to let this type of short-sighted caution obscure the real nature of the situation in which we presently find ourselves. Few great advancements have ever been made which did not involve risks and the possibility of failure. In this case, however, the chance of being unsuccessful is remote, and the potential for great benefits of no doubt.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on Petro-Can and to register my objection to the bill, which I will oppose as vigorously as possible.
Not so long ago an English philosopher said that "it is the business of the future to be dangerous". Our dwindling oil and gas supplies, and the failure of governments to do much to remedy the situation, provide sufficient grounds to justify that statement. According to the National Energy Board, by 1985 Canada will be too short of domestic oil to meet our demands in the west, much less take care of Ottawa, Montreal and eastern markets. This estimate is based on projections of new finds and the development of 500,000 barrels a day from oil sands.
Recent events showed how little government has guided us around this maze of problems; measures seem to be more cosmetic than substantive. The national energy conservation program revolving around voluntary co-operation to reduce gasoline consumption by cutting speed will not be very effective. Voluntary guidelines for lowering indoor temperatures, or consideration of improvements in mass transit or building insulation are, at best, of minor significance. Just a year ago the Canadian government boasted that we have exported $200 million worth of oil. Yet in 1975 Canada will be a net importer of oil. Obviously, we must curtail our exports if we are going to be in any way self-sufficient in oil.
Just what is the point of having a national petroleum company? In this highly controlled industry of oil and gas, controlled rigidly at the provincial level which dictates where drilling shall occur, regulates how much of the natural products may be taken from the well, and what the price should be at the wellhead, regulated once again by the federal government once the product leaves the province of origin, with the ability to restrict and prohibit export sales, the addition of a Crown corporation to involve itself in exploration, drilling, refining and marketing seems to be a waste of time, unless the government intends to socialize for the sake of socializing, and to control for the sake of controlling as a philosophy.
The record of this government in dealing with the oil and gas industry must appear to the outside world as ludicrous. The action of the federal government has been to slow down and eliminate private drilling and production in this country, at a time when the National Energy Board has warned of growing dependence on imported oil, when it is questioning exports at its current hearings on natural gas supplies, and is sounding the knell of supply shortfalls for the latter part of this decade, which may already be too late to remedy.
Surely in our present situation in the world there are much more important things to be done than starting a Petro-Can government corporation that will take years to get under way, and its best use in the short run will be to provide a large number of jobs at the taxpayers' expense.
In the activity of drilling, for instance, which is certainly the beginning of the development of an oil and gas field, in 1974 activity in Canada was down a good deal. This year industry sources are looking for a 25 per cent drop in activity as exploration budgets are slashed. The exodus of

drilling rigs and the people who go with them surely is cause for some alarm, particularly so because many of these rigs that have gone are of so-called deep-hole capacity. The number of active drilling rigs in Canada has fallen to the lowest level since 1966, according to the best industrial estimates, and in every part of Canada drilling activity is down. Whether this bill is supposed to stop the flight of drilling rigs from western Canada and to provide additional employment is not at all clear.
The obvious problem facing the oil and gas industry in Canada, and the reason for its decline, is the confrontation between the federal and provincial governments. With the price of oil at the wellhead at $6.50 a barrel, 20 per cent of that goes to the federal government, 50 per cent goes to the provincial government, and 30 per cent goes to the industry. In other words, of the basic price of crude oil, approximately 20 cents per gallon, the provincial and federal governments get 14 cents. Furthermore, in the process of refining, manufacturing and distributing, the federal and provincial governments reap additional tax benefits-for instance, the federal excise tax plus corporation taxes, as well as various other local and provincial taxes. I give these figures because I wish to make some comparison with another form of energy, that is, electricity generated by hydro power.
We are assured by scientists and economists that the world is probably entering the end of the gas and oil era, and that likely in the future we will depend on electricity developed from some other form of energy. In my hometown of Dauphin, Manitoba Hydro offers quite a good rate for the heating of homes, something like 114 cents per kilowatt. Reportedly this is going to go up shortly, something like a 15 per cent to 25 per cent increase. The cost of heating a house with fuel oil at the present rate, and the cost of heating a house with electricity are approximately the same, with some variation depending on the efficiency of the heating unit employed.
Manitoba is blessed with a large amount of hydro electric power, with a substantial amount still to be developed. Does Manitoba Hydro pay any corporation tax? Of course it does not, and it could not afford to, Mr. Speaker. Does it pay any royalties to the province of Manitoba? Of course it does not, and it does not pay any dividends to shareholders. It does not help to contribute directly to the provincial tax coffers in any form. It does not pay a federal excise tax, and it is fortunate to generate enough capital to expand its operations in order to carry on the business of providing new sources of power.
Even the bonds it must float every year, and usually this is in New York, to develop its plants, are guaranteed by the province of Manitoba, and to this extent they are a charge on the tax base of the people of Manitoba. In addition the federal government has involved itself in providing assistance to develop lines to carry high voltage electricity, to the tune of about a couple of hundred million dollars.
I have no reason to believe that Manitoba Hydro is not a well run organization, but I do think this points up the fact that, in respect of the final cost to the consumer who uses gas and oil, by far the greatest cost is in the form of the tax levied by federal and provincial governments. Provincial hydro electric companies are not able to con-
March 18, 1975

tribute to the tax base and are even net drawers on the taxpayer's purse under certain circumstances. This also points up the fact that the basic cost of gas and oil is much lower than the cost of a unit of hydro electric power could ever hope to be. Furthermore, nuclear power, as far as I am aware, is an expensive source of electricity, much more expensive than hydro electric power is ever likely to be.
It seems obvious that private industry is much more likely and capable of generating the activity needed to provide this country with a sure supply of oil and gas if it is given half a chance. The main stumbling block is the high level of taxation imposed on the industry by the two levels of government. If investment returns were adequate would we find the present exodus of drilling rigs to the south? Of course our neighbours to the south are not that much better off than we, and they are no more adept at promoting a suitable supply. Both nations seem to be involved in attempting to curtail any increase in the price of the producers for old oil, but they are both willing to pay nations across the water almost any amount they ask for oil, and are seemingly happy to do so.
If the price of oil and gas were raised, the companies would be paying enormous income taxes. If the normal taxation structure allowed too much money to remain in the hands of the oil companies then an excess profits tax could be levied. With the excess revenue the government could well institute a much more effective conservation plan, with alleviation of human suffering, particularly in respect of home heating oil. Surely this would have given a better basis to long-term planning and development of the energy resources required in the future. It makes no sense to scrap deliberately a system that has functioned reasonably well and has provided Canadians with a modest lead time in respect of national interests.
The minister has stated:
This does not mean that the government finds that Canada has not been well served by private enterprise in the petroleum industry. Private companies, whether Canadian or foreign-owned, have generally worked vigorously to develop our oil and gas resources, to create transportation systems for them and to efficiently refine and distribute oil products. The privately-owned Canadian oil industry has a good record of technical and managerial innovation.
This, coming from the minister, would certainly seem to belie the necessity of establishing this government company at the present time.
The minister also states that the bill contains authority to explore for, develop, and exploit hydrocarbon deposits within and without Canada, to carry out research and development projects related to hydrocarbons and other fuel, to engage in exploration, production, distribution and marketing of fuels and, finally, to negotiate and acquire petroleum products abroad.
This idea that a national oil company will buy better than a private company will need some explanation. For instance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) went to Venezuela about a year ago. After he left, the Venezuelan government raised the price and reduced production. When he went to Venezuela a few weeks ago the Venezuelan government again raised the price and reduced production. If he makes many more trips like this Venezuela will be out of business. Perhaps
Petro-Canada
he will be able to trade the Orinoco tar sands for the Athabasca tar sands.
There is not much evidence that a government company in the long run will be in a position to negotiate much better than a private company. Provision is made for authorized capital but little detail is given. Many questions must be answered. Does the federal government intend to acquire and lease provincial lands and set up its own rules, regulations and so on? Is this a means by which the right of ownership of provinces will be negated? Is this the intention of the government? Certainly Petro-Can, leasing and drilling within the provinces, and backed by the federal government, will want to be top dog over any provincial authority. Will it even want to adhere to any provincial regulations particularly if ordered not to do so by its federal boss? All these questions must be answered.
Now I should like to speak for a few moments about the problem of our balance of payments and how this relates to the oil situation at this time. A year ago we had a balance of approximately $200 million in oil trade in our favour, and yet this year we are faced with a deficit of approximately $500 million or $700 million. This amount could even be greater, and it is apparent that this situation could continue.
Today in the House the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated that we would have a balance of payments deficit of $4 billion to $5 billion. Surely this is an enormous sum. Are we to import money? He mentioned he hoped this would be solved by the balance of payments inflows, and presumably by investment money. Where will this money be obtained and where will it be invested? What about the government's plan to control foreign investment and the board which has been set up to phase out foreign investment which is not, so-called, for the good of Canada? Certainly this is a great problem.
The government has phased out all the oil drilling companies and the oil and gas wells it might have used to provide some much needed foreign exchange. Almost certainly we will be faced with the fact that we will have to develop Canadian trade dollars before many months or years have gone by. This balance of payments problem is a very large one which will affect all of us. It will reduce our level of activity. It will reduce the standard of living for our people, or at least prevent a rise in our standard of living.
By this bill the government has served notice that it has no confidence in private industry developing oil and gas reserves. By its taxation policies and by its failure to reach agreement with the producing provinces on taxation, it has shown little thought for the long-range viewpoint of the industry. I think Petro-Can can be considered as a forerunner for the complete takeover of the oil and gas industry by the government. It certainly will not in any way contribute to investment by private or mutual pension funds, the funds on which we rely for investment in this industry. So, Mr. Speaker, this is not a good bill, and I hope it will be defeated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) spoke on second reading of Bill C-8, to establish a national petroleum company. The

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
weak and misleading arguments he put forward in his speech on the bill indicate either a complete lack of understanding of how to achieve his stated energy objectives, or that the national petroleum company is part of a deliberate grand design to stifle and strangle a viable petroleum industry so that Petro-Can, with the Canadian taxpayers' dollars, can attempt a move into the void created when the private sector is forced to vacate.
The minister's opening words set the stage for his fallacious arguments. He stated that "the national interests now require a significant degree of federal public enterprise in the oil and natural gas area." He also said that the bill is a "most important element in the government's long term planning to secure adequate supplies of energy to meet our national needs ... at reasonable prices as well as a direct share in the wealth which development of our resources generates."
The minister has implied that the national oil company is the answer to adequate and reliable supplies of energy at reasonable prices for Canadians. On the basis of this phony argument, he and the government are deceiving the Canadian people in the hope that Canadians will buy this, and thus support the principle and the need for a national oil company. Most important, however, is the signal and warning throughout the minister's speech that fundamental changes in the free enterprise system are about to take place. The oil industry has in a few short years-and I hope the NDP member and the minister are listening- brought this country from a position of complete dependency on imported oil and gas to its place today where it is the only developed country in the world which can claim self-sufficiency in energy.

speechtext: How come we are not?

speechtext:
We are slipping away, and the British Columbia and Saskatchewan NDP governments are making a contribution to the pending shortfall.
Under a guise of nationalism and security of future energy supplies, this government is about to change, perhaps dramatically, a formula which succeeded at least until the government began to tamper with the marketplace and resource taxation policy. Of considerable concern, Mr. Speaker, is the effect that entry of a national oil company will have upon investment by the private sector.
There is real and legitimate concern by those in industry that, by reason of operating under different rules and special advantages relating to taxation, land acquisition and access to the collective confidential geological information of the whole industry, the Crown company will in a meaningful way further erode the ultimate achievement possible by private resource companies. This simply adds to the long list of uncertainties which face the oil and gas industry. There can be but one result-further uncertainty, further erosion of confidence and thus, further cutbacks in industry budgets. The greater the reduction in budgets by industry, the greater the apparent need for government investment of taxpayers' dollars.
These concerns are much greater as a result of the horrible track record of the government in the past two years. The simple fact is that the government is not trust-

ed. Since future energy reserves available to Canadians will be in direct proportion to the dollars invested, any cut back will reduce our reserves and thus our ability to produce in future years.
In summary then, Mr. Speaker, it is critical that the government spell out in full detail the answers to concerns expressed by the oil industry, for the crisis of future supply would be magnified many times if a further reduction took place in the activity of the private sector. What may have appeared to be a simple step taken by the government could seriously and adversely affect our already frightening energy prospects.
One of the realities of the 1970's is the increasing role that politics is playing in the energy policy-making of virtually every country in the world. In this unfortunate development, however, Canada is near the top of the list. The minister's remarks make it very clear that Petro-Canada will not be an oil company which will simply serve to search for reserves and increase Canadian presence. It is clearly going to be a tool of government which will be motivated by political expediency.
This is obvious from the minister's statement that the company's criterion may be modified in the terms of job opportunities or the development of particular parts of Canada, as he said. It is hard to believe that a national petroleum company would have any significant impact on increased employment benefits relative to existing oil companies unless the minister has in mind additional opportunities at large salaries for future defeated Liberal candidates.

speechtext: That is what the Tories do.

The white paper of June, 1973 stated "there are many areas in Canada with a petroleum potential which, for a variety of reasons, are not attractive to the private corporation". The cost of finding, developing and transporting oil to market from the most attractive areas of Canada is already exceedingly high. It appears that the government, for the sake of regional development or local politics, intends to look for oil and gas at any cost with public funds where chances of finding reserves may be remote.
It is a further programmed and planned folly by this government and this minister to direct the expenditure of funds of the national petroleum company in areas that are known to be less attractive areas for petroleum potential. A national oil company that is motivated by regional considerations would almost certainly be expending its dollars where the votes could be bought, and we all know in this House that this is not likely to be in western Canada.
The minister outlined in the House the factors which, in his words, "tipped the balance decisively in favour of federal entrepreneurship in the oil and energy industries". He pointed out that the government's energy white paper
March 18, 1975

produced in the spring of 1973 followed a long period of tranquillity and stability in domestic as well as international energy affairs. He went on to say that since that time changes have been radical. What the minister should have said, if he was speaking frankly, was that on the domestic scene in Canada it was during the long period of tranquility and stability that great accomplishments were realized by the oil and gas industries that brought our country to its enviable place of self-sufficiency. He should have said that during this period massive programs utilizing new technology, spending large sums of money and undertaken at great risk, were well under way in the Canadian Arctic and in off-shore areas of the east coast.
The minister's reference to "radical changes" which have taken place could only have been a reference to the actions of the federal government which, in turn, triggered so many protective reactions and moves by the provinces. It was these radical changes which were handed to the country by this Liberal government that have reduced the level of confidence in the oil and gas industries to its present very low level. The low level of confidence of energy investors today is the principal reason that our country's economic future is so seriously threatened.
As I have said in the House before, in a few short years Canada will be importing over 20 per cent of its oil needs, rising to over 50 per cent by 1985, unless drastic changes are made. I have pointed out to this House as well that the balance of payments problems in the years ahead are going to affect seriously the economic status of every Canadian.
The minister in his remarks on Bill C-8 had made a number of references to the concern of the government about the supply of oil and gas in the future. In fact, eight times in his short presentation he stressed the need for adequate supplies, secure supplies, expanding our supply potential, assuring long term future supply, assurance of supply continuity, and the pressing need for the development of resources. There is something very strange and sinister in the statements made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He has laid extreme emphasis on future energy supply, but his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), has all but killed a healthy industry with his tax measures.
Somebody is lying about the objectives of the government. On one hand we are being told that the government believes that the national interest now requires a significant degree of public enterprise to secure adequate supplies of energy to meet our national needs. On the other hand we were told on March 5, in the standing committee of the House, by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that he sees in Canada at present a healthy and vigorous oil industry progressing toward higher and higher levels of activity. The fact is that the reduction in expenditure by the industry in this year alone, due to the policies or lack of policies of this government, will amount to more than the entire capital of Petro-Can, which I understand is to try to make its funds last for some years. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that just the reduction in exploration expenditures by the private sector this year will be greater than the total capital proposed for the national oil company.
Petro-Canada
The minister as usual made a number of additional wild political claims which indicate how out of touch he is with the realities of the business world. I might say that I have seen very few ministers of the present government who do not fall significantly into that same category.
The minister's comments regarding joint ventures with smaller Canadian controlled firms seem to suggest that the purpose of the joint venture thrust in the bill is to assist the smaller Canadian controlled firms in providing funds for exploration in the frontier areas. Surely the objective of financing exploration in frontier areas could be achieved in far more efficient ways than by forming a national oil company. If the federal government is really concerned about the ability of the small Canadian controlled companies that finance exploration programs, I would suggest that the government could achieve its objective of encouraging these small companies by providing adequate incentives for frontier area exploration. If these adequate incentives are provided, smaller Canadian controlled companies will be better able to raise the necessary funds and continue their programs.
On the subject of frontier exploration, the minister and his government have been promising for at least five years that regulations for the Northwest Territories and federal government lands off-shore would be clarified in the near future. The minister has told me that in the House on several occasions. The land order which dealt with a certain key portion of the rules under federal lands was revoked on April 15, 1970. Thus just one month from now it will be five years. During this time the industry has continued to spend thousands of millions of dollars without any knowledge as to how the corridor lands and frontiers will be treated.

Petro-Canada
permits, and there has not been a federal land sale since 1969. This is just another example of the 180 degree effort this government is making in comparison with every other government in the world.
Surely the minister should provide immediately to the people of Canada an answer to this vital question of oil regulations. The absence of such regulations, however, is just a further reason why exploration activity is falling off. In case the minister does not know this, Panarctic has just sent to its shareholders material relating to budgets for 1976. These shareholders must by April 14, less than a month from now, respond regarding their willingness to be committed to the next round of financing. Undoubtedly the most farcical contradiction of all in the statements made by members of the government, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), is their unwillingness to recognize that since the oil industry began in Canada no meaningful incentives have been provided to Canadian citizens to invest in this important industry. Thus, in the absence of Canadian dollars, exploring companies, both foreign and Canadian, were forced to seek funds and partners in the United States and elsewhere. The high percentage of foreign ownership of our oil and gas industry is by design of the Liberal government. It has virtually assured the continuing foreign ownership which the government pretends to attack at every opportunity.
Considerable emphasis has been placed by the minister in his speech on the creation of a national oil company by the government for, in his words, it will bring to the petroleum sector the social benefits to Canadians of the pride, satisfaction and confidence of owning a portion of this important Canadian industry. I see the minister is leaving. He cannot bear hearing the truth. He cannot face up to this.
Again the minister conveniently overlooks the fact that 150 or more independent oil companies are operating in Canada. A large percentage of these are Canadian owned or controlled. I am sorry to say that many of these Canadian companies are forced to spend a percentage of their budgets outside Canada, and many are being forced to move away. Immediate steps must be taken by the government to encourage the corporate growth and strength of this group of companies in Canada for our own good.
The policies of the government, however, in the last two years have penalized our own Canadian oil companies which form a significant part of the industry. It should be borne in mind that these companies in recent years have done some 80 per cent of the exploratory drilling in the western provinces. But equally as important, they make up the Canadian segment of the industry which is such an important part of the policy which is claimed by the minister to be important to the government.
The best solution for all would be the emergence of independent and strong investor owned Canadian oil companies numbering as many as possible. It is necessary, [Mr. Bawden.l
however, to create favourable tax policies, otherwise this important sector in the industry will be the first to die and the first to disappear.
Our present Canadian owned and directed corporations are examples of just how little pride, satisfaction and confidence have been inspired in Canadians by their presence. Canadians now own, subject to outstanding loans of $4 billion, a railroad, the CNR; a postal service; an airline, Air Canada; the St. Lawrence Seaway; a heavy water plant at Glace Bay; a communications network in the CBC, and a Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which is looking after our native people. Have any of these government undertakings generated pride, satisfaction and confidence in Canadians? How can one believe that government entry into the exceedingly complex petroleum industry will be any more successful or profitable than the government's history of action to date?
Social satisfaction will not provide the capital, technology and long term positive energy policy required to meet Canada's energy requirements. Who knows, the national oil company might be as successful as the Post Office.

He goes on to say that the obvious interest to be served, the Canadian interest, is that of importing at lower cost than private companies are able to do.
I defy the minister to find a country in the world which will sell oil to this country at any bargain price, even if the minister's own sweet personality were present on the scene to assist in the bargaining. The minister also stated that such a company would offer greater assurance of supply continuity. Most of the state oil companies of exporting countries have stepped in by way of take-overs of existing reserves which are often projected to have a life of 25 years or 50 years or more. Thus further successful exploration is not particularly critical. Much the converse is true in Canada where the national petroleum company would be commencing operations with no oil and no people, just a government. In addition, Canada has approximately ten years of oil supply left from current fields.

speechtext: Not a bit!

Canada has approximately ten years of oil supply left from current fields, and due principally to political actions and interference by this government our country is now working on its very modest inventory against that date projected by the National Energy Board in the near future when Canadians will be forced to go short.
A state company, for the very reason that it is a state company, must bear the nation's nationality, its immigration policy, its trade policy, its defence commitments, and so on. For that reason it is exceedingly difficult for a national petroleum company to play an effective role with petroleum companies of other countries. The petroleum companies, as they are multi-national, are far more likely to be efficient, flexible and businesslike in finding, developing, moving and selling oil. In any event, other departments of government could perform this function, were it ever required. This, Mr. Speaker, was demonstrated during the Arab oil embargo last year. There were many countries, such as Holland, that would not have received their required supply or in many cases any supply of oil. It was only possible due to the flexibility of those large companies that were trading oil, in many cases on the high seas, where swaps and switches were made to keep the fires burning and the industries of the world moving.
How then, Mr. Speaker, should the government achieve its objective of collecting for Canadians their share of the wealth from the oil and gas industry? If a review is made of dollar receipts from oil production since 1947, considerable insight is provided into who got the wealth.
Between 1947 and the end of 1974 the Alberta government received by way of Crown sales, rentals and royalties just over $6 billion. To the end of 1973, approximately the same period of time, the petroleum industry spent approximately $21 billion and received back by way of income, before tax, $21.3 billion. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it has taken the industry as a group almost 30 years to recover its investment and show a slight favourable balance.
Of course there are successful companies and there are unsuccessful companies, and members of the NDP constantly point to those that have been successful. They have not had much to say about those that have not been successful, although perhaps their first candidate may be Saskoil and other associations sponsored by the Socialist government of Saskatchewan. The oil and gas industry is continuing to re-invest and it is likely that this net favourable return to industry will not climb in the near future to a significantly greater positive balance.
It seems very clear to me, Mr. Speaker, that the way to succeed financially in the oil business is to lease out, farm out, and utilize every other measure at hand to entice others to spend money on your land, while at the same time collecting a reasonable level of royalty. Something over 25 per cent of the total funds realized by the province of Alberta were as a result of Crown sales of lands which
Petro-Canada
were returned to the government subsequent to discoveries. These lands were offered for sale by competitive bid to all comers. There was no risk to the province of Alberta. Its return of some $6 billion over this period, since 1947, compares to the one-third billion or one-half billion dollars to the oil and gas industry cumulatively. Even to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and hon. members opposite it should be clear how governments, or anybody who holds control of the ultimate land leases, should deal if they have any interest in participating in the wealth.
It is interesting to note that the United States government has taken in something in the order of $5 billion in land sales off Louisiana during the past three years. Some of these individual sales brought in cash bids totalling well over a billion dollars, some close to a billion and a half. In a recent one the total was $1,400 million. It seems to me that receiving this kind of cash on the front end prior to any determination of whether oil and gas reserves exist, while at the same time collecting a royalty and income tax on the ultimate profit, could hardly be bettered in finding a way for Canadians to participate in the wealth, and without risk of taxpayers' dollars.
I read recently about a purchase which was made by a group of large companies in the Gulf of Mexico off the state of Florida for over $300 million. I later learned that some four dry holes have been drilled on the structure underlying the lease, and in all probability after total expenditures of close to $400 million the exercise will be a complete write-off. That, Mr. Speaker, is the way that the federal government should be involving Canadians in the oil and gas industry, by collecting the bonus bid and farming out the leases, but not by taking the risk. This practice has been followed in Alberta, not only under a Conservative government but also for many years under a Social Credit government.
A last but important area that needs to be considered by this House and by the standing committee is the list of powers to be accorded to this national petroleum corporation. Since I have mentioned the costs of exploring in the Gulf of Mexico-and I might say that many areas of the world require substantial advance cash bonuses-I note with considerable interest that the national petroleum Canada company is to have powers to go abroad and operate outside Canada. I ask why? Could it be that the national petroleum company has also foreseen and is beginning to understand that the climate in this country is not attractive to investors with petroleum dollars? I hope that later in this debate the minister will tell us what percentage of the company's funds will be invested in foreign countries.
The national oil company may, according to the minister, participate in the transportation of petroleum products. The minister says transportation is a natural extension to the company's efforts "by assuring that the energy resources it helped to find and develop are brought to the Canadian consumer without undue delay and at least cost". Mr. Speaker, I doubt if anyone in Canada who examined this statement would accept it as either fact or truth. We have only to look today at the significant role the government is already playing in transportation, and to check the record for deliveries. Western farmers have

Petro-Canada

This has greatly harmed our international reputation. For the minister to say that the government might move oil or gas without delay and at the least cost is just another exaggeration being presented to the Canadian people.
I read recently a comparison which I thought interesting. In 1956 the oil industry moved by pipeline a 300 pound barrel of oil from Edmonton to Sarnia for 64 cents. By 1973 this transportation cost had been reduced by 25 per cent, to 48 cents per barrel. During this same period the federal postal service cost to transport a post card increased 100 per cent from four cents to eight cents, and the delivery period, as everyone knows, for the Post Office is completely uncertain. The minister was reported last year in the press to have stated that the new corporation may nationalize existing oil companies. If, in fact, it is the basic purpose of the government to increase exploration and development, how can this be accomplished by the national oil company if its funds are utilized for acquisitions rather than for new exploration activity?
A great deal of emphasis is placed in the bill on the powers which the company will have to lend money to persons dealing with a corporation, and to those proposing to do business with the corporation. In addition it will be permitted to endorse promissory notes, to guarantee loans for others, and will have many other such powers. I am reminded of the story of the man from Calgary who visited his friend in the cattle business. The friend had a very high priced bull and the city visitor had gone out to see it. When he arrived at his friend's ranch he noticed that the bull was hitched up to and pulling a plough. He was very surprised. He asked his rancher friend why this very high priced prize bull was hitched up to a plough. The rancher replied, "I just want him to learn that the cattle business ain't all romance." The company will also be empowered to invest in ventures related to exploration, which I presume could mean seismograph contracting, drilling contracting, or presum-
[Mr. Bawden.l

This country has been well served by the oil and gas industry. Anyone can see that the companies have not brought this situation upon themselves; they have been forced into it by the action of the federal governments, in concert with provincial governments, making it impossible for them to set aside adequate pools of capital.
The attitude taken by the government is a ridiculous one. It says the companies cannot provide sufficient capital yet it ignores the fact that it is the governments concerned which have created the problem. The problem having been created, we are asked to approve the setting up of yet another bureaucracy in an attempt to solve it. No doubt this will be of great benefit to the taxpayers of the country-I say that ironically because I cannot imagine any situation more likely to cause shortages or oblige them to pay higher prices for petroleum. That is the role upon which the government has embarked.
Later in his speech the minister tells us that another reason this capital might not be available is that the companies are faced with "attractive investment opportunities and geological possibilities abroad." But why should they be offered more attractive investment possibilities abroad? What is wrong with the investment possibilities in this country? Why doesn't the government create a climate which can compete with the climate anywhere else?

Hear, hear!

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: There is no incentive at all to be successful in Canada any more.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

speechtext: The Minister of National Revenue is really an amazing person. He shows abysmal ignorance of the whole subject. He talks as though the hon. member for Calgary South has any control over his own rigs in that respect. My hon. friend does not drill on his own property. He responds to requests from customers, and if they do not want to drill in Canada I suppose the hon. gentleman would like him to leave his iron to rust here, go out of business, throw people out of work, and pay no more taxes to the federal government. subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: If I may, I would just like to clarify the situation for the benefit of many members opposite who have taken various opportunities to make uninformed remarks. The company in which I was involved, and in which I still have an interest, is one of the few drilling contracting firms in Canada which has not moved a rig out of this country in the last two years since the government messed things up.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for clarifying the situation. I wonder how long it can last though, because the level of drilling has now fallen to the level of 1966, nine years ago. In the last year or year and a half there has been a phenomenal drop in activity, and it is probably going to get worse.
I was talking about the investment climate, Madam Speaker. Canada has not been made the best place in which to invest, and this reminds me of another problem created by the activities of the government and its predecessors. I refer to the situation where the government said it needed a Foreign Investment Review Board because so much Canadian industry was owned by foreigners and we had to bring a halt to this.
The petroleum industry is held up as an example. The government says that because it is 90 per cent foreign controlled, this is bad. If it is bad, why did it allow the situation to develop? The government has had a tax regime in this country that has made it impossible for Canadians to own or develop their own resources. Then when development does take place by so-called foreigners, the government sets up a Foreign Investment Review Board to control it. This is another example of creating a problem and then setting up some silly, one might say stupid, government body to solve the problem.
The minister also uses the excuse that there are uncertainties about the importation of oil and that it will be necessary for the government to deal with foreign owned oil companies in order to acquire sufficient supplies for Canadians. It does not display much confidence in the activities of Petro-Can when the minister says in one breath that it will solve our supply and price problem, and in the next breath says it is needed because we must deal with foreign owned oil companies in order to assure

supply. I wish the minister would get on track and tell us exactly what he is going to do with this bill.
Why do we need a new organization to import oil? We already have the Canada Commercial Corporation which is 100 per cent state owned. I might say its record is not too good so far as its attempts to solve our supply problem last year is concerned. Hon. members will recall that it bought some Roumanian, Hungarian or Bulgarian oil, or oil from one of the Balkan states, which is so full of sulphur that it cannot be used, and we ended up losing $14 million to $15 million on the deal. Is this the kind of government action that is going to assure our supplies of oil at the lowest possible price? First of all you cannot use it; secondly, it cost two or three times the price of oil that could be obtained somewhere else.
The government has shown no capacity to supply energy at a proper price to Canadians. At the same time companies have supplied surplus oil-oil which was coming out of their ears-and natural gas which they did not know what to do with at the lowest possible price. If I were to criticize those companies in any way I would say that they kept prices too low for too long. This has not been good for the conservation of a depleting resource but the record of the industry on the whole has been too good.
Then the minister goes on to say that it would give Canadians a great deal of pride to have Petro-Can. The hon. member for Calgary South also referred to other Crown corporations. If the government were sponsoring a corporation the shares of which are available to Canadians, and Canadians had a good prospect of receiving a dividend, then they might have some sort of pride in the organization. But that is not what is being proposed in this mess that is before us. This corporation will issue 100 shares which will be owned exclusively by the government and which are non-transferrable. So how can anyone have any sort of connection with an abortion like that?
I can cite Air Canada as an example. How many people are proud of that organization? Certainly I do not talk to many who are. That is a corporation that pays no taxes yet runs up deficits. At the same time other organizations operating in the same field pay taxes, their shareholders pay tax on the corporations' dividends, and they provide better service to boot.
The minister says that he will have an honest company which will be subject to the disciplines of the profit and loss statement. The most charitable word I can think of to describe that is baloney. I do not care how thin you slice it, it is still baloney.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Garbage is a better word.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
I can think of better words too, but I will be getting into unparliamentary language. This bill is not worth a pinch of the proverbial. On top of saying that we will have all these wonderful low prices and assured supplies, the minister is going to use this corporation as a vehicle for regional development. I ask you, Madam Speaker, does this mean that Petro-Can is going to drill oil wells where there is no oil just to make work and build up the economy in an area? You drill oil wells where you expect to find oil, not where you are trying to build up the local economy. If this company is being formed for the purpose of artificially stimulating the local economies of
March 18, 1975

various regions in this country, then it may as well be called-

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: An OFY grant.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

-a super duper OFY grant, as suggested by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). Or else it is going to be the ultimate in pork barrelling. I can imagine during the next election campaign Liberal candidates saying, "If you elect me I will make sure that Petro-Can drills an oil well in this constituency". The whole thing is just beyond belief.
Then the minister goes on to say that this corporation is going to have a great social conscience and is going to train the native people of this country.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Perhaps it is going into the dredging business.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

I do not know whether we are dealing here with a vocational school or an oil company. Either you have an efficiently run oil company that is designed to get oil out of the ground at the cheapest possible price in as large a quantity as possible, or you have a vocational school. I do not think an oil company should be used as a vehicle for training the labour force. Certainly we should have training and retraining programs for our native people, and for all others in this country who require them. But let us not do this through the use of a Crown corporation that is supposed to provide oil and gas in abundant supplies at low prices.
Then the minister makes a comment about being subject to the disciplines of an operational statement and the balance sheet. As my hon. friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) characterizes that, it is just garbage.

speechtext: Toward the end of his remarks he says that there may be areas of exploration not undertaken by private sectors because commercial returns are not easily defined by the corporations involved or because they are deemed to be too far distant. We have had a situation for the last four or five years during which there have been absolutely no ground rules on which the number of companies operating in the Arctic could rely.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speechtext: They change them every second day.

speechtext:
They did not change them because they did not have any. They abolished the land use regulations that were established in 1961, and have not replaced them with anything, so in actual fact the hundreds of millions of dollars spent there by the private sector in the past four or five years have been spent totally on speculation because companies do not know to what rules they will be subject. I do not think there is any evidence that the private sector in this country is anything but cautious about how it spends its exploration money. I think these
Petro-Canada
companies are to be commended for spending the money they have in spite of the lack of any ground rules set down by the government. In any event the minister does not think they will continue, and I suppose this is a normal thought. I am sure he would not operate on the basis of the faith displayed by this government over the past number of years.
The minister also said there might also be areas of exploration which are not being pursued by the private sector because of the financial burdens involved, and these are cases where the national company would carry out exploration activities on its own. I do not think the private companies have shown any evidence of behaving in that way. I suggest that it is not a function of this proposed company to explore in the most costly and least likely areas to produce oil and natural gas, but that seems to be the implication of what the minister is saying he wants it to do. Again I say I cannot go for that type of policy. The minister has shown no practical sense at all in the drafting of this bill, or in his ideas put forward in respect of this proposed company and what it is supposed to do.
The minister has also suggested that it is bad that the petroleum industry is 90 per cent foreign owned. I suggest it is better to have an industry that is 90 per cent foreign owned than to have no industry at all, and that would have been the case if they had not come into Canada. There certainly never were any policies of this government or its predecessor to give Canadians any break at all in respect of the development of their own resources. There is still no indication that the government wants to give any incentive to Canadians to develop their own resources, except through the direct route of socialism.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: It is.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
It is, is it? I find it rather strange that this creature called Sask Oil, which has now established rather elaborate offices in the city of Calgary, is so active in Alberta buying gas from that province at the price Alberta wants to charge, when it will not make the same arrangements with producers of natural gas in the province of Saskatchewan. I find it a rather strange and unusual attitude that the people of Saskatchewan will go to Alberta and pay what the market there demands, but will not give the same deal to the producers who are finding and producing in the province of Saskatchewan. That does not seem to make sense.

March 18, 1975
Petro-Canada
The final solution of the government appears to be nationalization of the industry for the benefit of Canadians, even though we have numerous examples that nationalization does not work.
One of the most objectionable parts of the minister's statement is his reference to how the Canadian oil companies, which he says are largely foreign owned, treat their employees. He states, and I quote:
People are a company's most important resource and the Canadian petroleum industry has developed over the years a highly competent group of professionals who have become experts in all phases of industry operations including its management. The majority of these are employed by foreign-owned companies. The corporation will offer opportunities which are commensurate in challenge and scope, and as its role may ultimately be just as diverse as those of some large international companies, it will provide a good training ground for Canadians wishing to link their careers with the oil industry in the service of Canada.
I should think that all employees of existing oil companies are quite proud of the job they have done in serving Canada, making this a surplus area with low cost fuel. I resent greatly the implication that these existing companies are in fact grinding the faces of the poor in their relations with their employees, and that it now is a fortunate thing the government of Canada has come along with a vehicle to save them from the clutches of foreign owned corporations. That is unworthy of the minister, and it is at total variance with the facts. It has been my personal experience that these so-called foreign controlled oil companies have had exceptionally good personnel policies and relations.
So we are left with a proposal that is contradictory in its terms, and with no evidence that this will solve our problems. It is part of government policy to ensure future energy requirements. It is interesting to note that this is probably the only country in the world that is still subsidizing the use of gasoline by its citizens. That is a rather peculiar way to approach a situation in which we can see a shortfall in this depleting resource in the future. Nevertheless the government's policy is completely contradictory, with nothing going in one direction. I think it is a shame that this is the only industrialized area in the world not experiencing an upturn in exploration activity for oil and natural gas at the present time. In fact the converse is true. Our exploration activity has fallen to the 1966 level. The government should be doing something to create the proper atmosphere so that we can return to the conditions that created our former favourable position.
We have seen an admission of defeat by the government in the recent announcement that it will have to cut off oil exports very shortly. This will create problems in respect of balance of payments, and other difficulty in respect of our economy. I see nothing in the statement of the minister to show that the government has any idea about how to get back on the right track. This idea certainly is not the answer.
Many people have said that how much good or damage this proposed vehicle could cause will depend on how it is used. I suggest there is no guarantee concerning how it will be used. I would hate to see this vehicle established because then it would be available for my New Democratic

friends, and their type of inspiration, if they ever got hold of the levers of government. I can well imagine what they would do if this type of organization were in existence. So in conclusion I say, as I said at the beginning, that I hope this little baby of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will be stillborn.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am particularly pleased to speak this evening, and probably also tomorrow afternoon, on this bill because I believe it is one of the more important bills to come before this parliament. This is the sixtieth Crown corporation to be created, if it is created.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope the record clearly shows that the applause came from the Liberal government benches, because I think it is time the people of Canada understood that the official opposition is the only party in the House which is standing up to oppose more public intervention in the private sector.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in introducing this bill said one thing with which I agree. Let me repeat it. This appears at page 4036 of Hansard. At that time the minister stated:
We harbour no illusions that establishment of a national petroleum company is likely to lead to early and spectacular results in terms of massive energy- development or financial success. I want the House to know that we are going into this venture in full realization of the fact that the hazards of exploration risk, technical and commercial uncertainty await this venture.
I say it is important not only that the House be told what the minister has stated but that the people of Canada be told what he has stated.
I referred to this as being the sixtieth Crown corporation to be inflicted on this nation. Let us take a look at the record of some of these Crown corporations that the government members have applauded so wholeheartedly. Let us start alphabetically with Air Canada. I would recommend that members on the government side pick up the new issue of "The National Finances" for 1974-75, which is published by the Canadian Tax Foundation. They should read it because it has a complete record concerning the Crown corporations about which they are overjoyed. I shall begin with Air Canada. The net profit of Air Canada for 1973 amounted to $6.1 million, down from the 1972 profit of $8.6 million. Federal loans to Air Canada totalled $253.8 million at March 31, 1974.
Next we have Canadian Arsenals Limited, a real beauty. It is shown here that financial statements for the corporation's year ending March 31, 1974, reflect a loss of $1.8 million on sales of $4.6 million. At March 31, 1974, loans to and investments in Canadian Arsenals Limited stood at $3.5 million.
Here is another real beauty, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Prior to 1953 the CBC deprived part of its revenue from a radio receiving fee. The report goes on to describe how that fee was abolished and substituted by
March 18, 1975

direct appropriation from the treasury. On March 31, 1974, the equity account stood at $1.8 million. Advances to the corporation for capital expenditures at the same date totalled $197.9 million, and working capital $9.6 million. In short we have a description of the almost unbelievable loss position the CBC has incurred over the years. I would recommend that these hon. members who so blindly support the government compare the record of the CBC with the record of any of the similar private, networks in the United States or Canada to see whether they should be proud of the financial results of the CBC.
Let me touch on the Canadian Commercial Corporation. Here we have a corporation which had gross expenditures of $7.7 million in 1973-74 and gross revenues of $2.1 million.
