subtopic: HEALTH-EFFECT OF POVERTY ON CHILDREN-SUGGESTED CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON ADOPTION OF FOOD PROGRAM
HEALTH-EFFECT OF POVERTY ON CHILDREN-SUGGESTED CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON ADOPTION OF FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I chose tonight to follow up on my question of March 10 to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) because I am really bothered by the result of the study on "Poor Kids" by the National Council on Welfare. It is impossible for me to understand why 1.6 million Canadian children are living in poverty when we take into account the wealth of our nation and the percentages related in the report. For example the highest proportion was in my province of Newfoundland where over 45 per cent of our children are in families with incomes below the poverty line.
Similar figures relate to other provinces, such as 42 per cent in the Northwest Territories, 37.3 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 38.4 per cent in Saskatchewan, and so the list goes on. One finds it sickening to read about some of the actual cases and the conditions under which they exist. I can say only that I can support these facts from my personal experience.
But the question we have to resolve is how to correct this embarrassing situation. The minister had indicated, and rightly so, that from a constitutional point of view the responsibility lies with the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan. I realize, as he indicated in his answer, that social services are now under study. He also said
Adjournment Debate
recently that he hopes that we will see a guaranteed annual income by 1976.
We already have a pretty good family allowance program which nationally amounts to $22.08 per child per month, and two provinces go beyond that amount to $41.68 in Quebec and $33.60 in Alberta.
Social assistance payments have increased over the years, and evidently our social security benefits compare favourably with the rest of the world.
Nevertheless, Madam Speaker, in spite of all our generous programs something must be drastically wrong with the direction of effort of many provinces and of the federal government when we see these startling and sickening figures. We must stop brushing off the problem with the stock answer that it is the responsibility of the provinces, and we must take the lead in correcting this disease of poverty.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in a motion he introduced recently recommended that the report should be required reading for all members of parliament. I agree with him, but I think it might be worthwhile to list a few of the pertinent points contained in the report.
The report states that, first, poor children are more likely to miss school due to illness, to be victims of home accidents, and to exhibit hearing and speech impairment.
Second, disadvantaged children are more apt to contact rheumatic fever, hepatitis, meningitis or tuberculosis.
Third, undernourished children are retarded in their height and weight development, suffer from physical and mental retardation, and a greater percentage of them has a history of diabetes. This happens in spite of the vast medical insurance plans which have been in existence for years.
The study refers to the lack of medical research in the search for solutions to the effects of poverty among children. I do not have the time to list some of the more pertinent points which they make with regard to medical research.
All this is happening in our wealthy country at the same time as medical costs reach uncontrollable proportions. We now have another report, to go along with all the others such as the Senate poverty report, namely, the nutrition survey, to indicate the alarming situation which exists with regard to our youth.
I do not say that the answers are simple, but it is obvious that we are trying to correct the problems experienced by our youth after the fact rather than at the right time.
The report makes a very valid point concerning how the physical and mental development of the fetus can be affected by the inadequacy of the mother's diet during pregnancy because she is poor and cannot afford nutritious food, with the result that the child pays the price of that poverty in stunted health even before it is born.
I recommend to the minister, first, that this matter hold high priority in his further meetings with provincial ministers of health. Second, I recommend that our priorities change with regard to our physical fitness programs so that greater attention is paid to physical development
March 18, 1975

Adjournment Debate
rather than to the achievement of excellence in a few children's sports with restricted participation. I am a strong advocate of our physical fitness program, but we must change our priorities because it is the weaker person who needs most leadership, guidance and coaching so that he will grow up to be a more healthy citizen. If we can provide many programs such as the OFY, or student exchange programs, if we can ask our youth to participate with initiative in many other citizen oriented programs, why in the world can we not provide a program whereby organizations in conjunction with school boards can supply nutritious food supplements in schools?
I feel very embarrassed when I receive letters such as this one from a school board. It reads:
Thank you tor your efforts on our behalf. Believe me they are deeply appreciated even though the results of your efforts have come to nought. The supplementary diet program for the schools under our board in Corner Brook area is functioning on a restrictive basis with funds supplied by two local parishes, and two local organizations.
I might point out that it is very difficult to secure funds for any ongoing project because people think that government should furnish funds.
He goes on in his frustration and finishes by saying that maybe he should tell them that the hungry children are "doing dope":
... then we could get funds to help "solve the problem". Maybe we could get some of the surplus eggs and chickens for a lunch program but that would no doubt upset the market price or some damn fool thing.
This is the frustration school boards and teachers are facing.
Finally, Madam Speaker, if such a large percentage of our population is composed of children, as indicated in the report, when we face these alarming problems which should be in the mind of every member of parliament, I think it is time and it is vital that the government appoint a full time minister of youth so that we can direct the efforts required to develop the more important segment of our society-

subtopic: HEALTH-EFFECT OF POVERTY ON CHILDREN-SUGGESTED CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON ADOPTION OF FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to refer the hon. member to the answer given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) on March 10, 1975. The answer is as follows:
... this matter comes under provincial jurisdiction. All social services are now under study with the provinces within the context of the social welfare review.
I would also like to add some supplementary remarks to the answer given to the hon. member.
First, it should be understood that there is no lack of nutritious food in this country. Recently the department moved to strengthen an already strong situation by proposing that the restoration of certain nutrients to staple foods and substitutes for staple foods be made mandatory. I refer specifically to the addition of vitamin D to all milk, vitamin A to all skimmed and partly skimmed milk, vitamin C to fruit drinks, and B vitamins and iron to flour.

Second, the nutrition Canada survey, which examined more than 4,000 school age children in the provinces, found little or no evidence of nutrient deficiency, certainly none which would be expected to prevent participation in school activities.
There is great interest throughout the country in school lunch programs and the quality of food available in schools. While I am pleased to note this interest, I would stress that there is a need to evaluate both present and proposed programs. The health protection branch of the department is currently collaborating with the government of Alberta in just such an evaluation of a new school lunch program in northern Alberta. They have offered similar assistance to the evaluation of programs in Manitoba and British Columbia. Only by such evaluation can we be sure that dollars spent on school lunch programs are not misspent.
Finally, the federal-provincial nutrition committee has undertaken the preparation of guidelines for the development of school lunch programs which will be available to all school and health officials. I will send the hon. member a copy if he so wishes.

subtopic: SPORTS-HOCKEY-SUGGESTION AMATEUR ASSOCIATIONS NOT SIGN CHILDREN TO CONTRACTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
SPORTS-HOCKEY-SUGGESTION AMATEUR ASSOCIATIONS NOT SIGN CHILDREN TO CONTRACTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Thursday I raised a question in this House, and it was directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I asked the following question:
In view of the fact that the minister was approached last year with respect to the case of 16 year old Michael Laffrade of Toronto who was prevented from playing hockey because he had signed a contract with an amateur team, and in view of the fact that the minister had expressed outrage and incredulity at the effects of that contract, and in view of the fact that the minister on the program "Ombudsman" had promised to speak to the CAHA about this situation, would he inform the House if he has contacted the CAHA and instructed it and its affiliated bodies to cease and desist from forcing children to sign contracts or forms which restrict their opportunities for playing hockey?
I further asked:
In view of the fact that many more cases similar to that of Michael Laffrade have surfaced this winter, will the minister inform the House as to what steps he is prepared to take to ensure that children do not become embroiled in legal disputes in the pursuit of voluntarily playing amateur sports in this country?
The minister preferred to duck the issue by repeating that he had contacted the CAHA, and he said nothing else.
The CAHA is the governing body for amateur hockey in this country. Participating players must sign CAHA registration forms to be able to play hockey in Canada. Because of its monopoly on amateur hockey, if you do not play for one of the CAHA teams you do not play hockey at all.
It is this registration card which has created a very inhuman and most undesirable form of slavery. In fine print above the signature of the child are the following words: "I hereby agree to abide by all the rules, regulations and decisions of the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association."
What about the rules? One would think that these rules are pretty easy to come by. They are as scarce to obtain as gold these days. They are not easily available to the
March 18, 1975

players, and indeed most of the children do not know what they are signing, and neither do their parents.
For your information, Madam Speaker, there are 174 pages of rules, 36 pages for the CAHA, 100 pages for the OHA and 38 pages for the MTHL-the young Metro-Toronto Hockey League. Among other things one rule forbids any team from signing or even trying out a player who was with another club the previous season, as long as that club has a team in the player's age division. It runs a minimum of two years, the year he plays and the following year. Thus he is indentured to the team.
Another rule establishes boundaries for teams, and players who live within those boundaries must play for the team within that boundary or get a release. Another rule gives the league the authority to specify which team a child will play for outside his boundary. Some children and their parents have tried to defy this slave trade and have sought recourse through the courts. But here again the CAHA has a rule, rule 145, which states that anyone doing so is liable to an automatic indefinite suspension unless the court finds that the CAHA acted contrary to the rules of what the CAHA terms "natural justice".
The comments of Mr. Gordon Juckes, executive director of CAHA, are rather eye-opening. He says:
Where you have a voluntary organization whose members belong only because they want to, it seems only sensible that people abide by the decisions of their fellow members. You shouldn't take an internal fight to the courts. It would be the same if you were a member of a golf club. The sport should be allowed to settle its own problems.
It is fairly obvious then that the CAHA is an association of teams rather than players, and players are owned by teams, and the rules are those which the team management adopts. The CAHA is all heart, and Mr. Juckes is filled with understanding when he says:
In my 20 years with the CAHA, I've never seen the rule against people going to the courts used. Last year, one boy wanted a transfer from Ontario to British Columbia, which both the branch and the CAHA refused to give. He went to court and got an injunction. We didn't suspend him. He went and played in Victoria just as he wanted.
It is quite clear that amateur sport is highly organized and professionally administered with only one aim in mind-prepare players for the professional leagues. There is much talk of playing for enjoyment, physical exercise, and personal development. Indeed the federal government has recognized this in legislation entitled the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act.
Section 3 of this act states:
The objects of this act are to encourage, promote and develop fitness and amateur sport in Canada ...
This section also permits the minister in his pursuance of the objects of this act to "assist, co-operate with and enlist the aid of any group interested in furthering the objects of this act".
Several questions arise over this matter, Madam Speaker, which I find very difficult to understand, and I hope whoever answers can clarify them for me. First, when a child signs those registration cards, is that a legal binding document, especially in view of the fact that these players are minors? Second, if a minor's signature on a contract is worthless, why is the CAHA allowed to use it to cow
Adjournment Debate
children and their parents into submission? Third, why does the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is responsible for amateur sport in Canada, not intervene and instruct the CAHA to cease and desist? After all, the minister certainly did not hesitate to intervene in keeping out an American league football team from Toronto.
Why do children have to sign any contracts at all? If the philosophy is "participaction" at this level, and it should jolly well be, then that becomes the reason for the team to exist.
What percentage of the children who start at the squirt level of hockey in Canada are still playing hockey at the midget level? I suspect that the percentage is very low indeed.
Some provinces have undertaken studies into hockey and have come up with recommendations for the creation of provincial hockey councils, or ombudsmen, to oversee amateur hockey. Probably these are worth-while suggestions, but I think the most immediate step is to eliminate this particular practice of contract signing by minors. Perhaps it may just motivate us to make participation much more of an enjoyable experience for our children.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REFUSAL OF CORPORATION TO SUPPLY TRANSCRIPT OF PROGRAM "TEN LOST YEARS"
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REFUSAL OF CORPORATION TO SUPPLY TRANSCRIPT OF PROGRAM "TEN LOST YEARS"
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I never thought I would have to rise in my place and demand that the government order the publicly-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to stop broadcasting pornography and smut.
On February 3 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), the minister responsible to the House for the CBC, if he would see that any future programs scheduled on CBC would be cancelled if they were no less insulting and of no higher quality than the show billed as "The Ten Lost Years".
The minister said simply that he would make my representation known to the corporation. The minister must have known that that would not answer my question, nor would it settle the issue that I raised. I did not ask the minister if he would make my representation known to the CBC. I could have done that myself. What I asked the minister to do was to take some action to ensure that CBC programming would be made more acceptable to the people whose tax money is used to run the corporation.
On February 13 the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) asked the Secretary of State similar questions concerning CBC programming, and the minister replied that it is the policy of the government not to instruct the corporation. I think that we all have a right to ask who does instruct the CBC in the name of the Canadian people if it is not their government.

I do not know of any government agency or Crown corporation which is not instructed and monitored by the government. I had always been under the impression, Madam Speaker, that this was one of the roles of ministers of the Crown. If there are any government corporations which are not monitored and instructed by the appropriate ministers, then it is time to find out which ones they are and to bring them under the control of parliament without further delay.
The Secretary of State, Madam Speaker, is well aware that it has never been accepted policy to turn a publicly-funded agency or corporation loose and allow it to function as it pleases. The mere fact that public money is involved not only makes such a policy unacceptable, it makes it illegal, and I should not have to make that point to the minister.
The point I am making now, and will continue to make until I get some action, is that no broadcasting facilities in Canada can be allowed to operate without some degree of continuing scrutiny and instruction by the appropriate government minister. The broadcasting medium in any country has a tremendous influence on public attitudes and views, and it has the power to mould public and private morality. This power must be used with restraint, and it must be used in the best interests of the majority of the people.
John Hirsh, the head of CBC television drama, told the Commons broadcasting committee this week that CBC has a responsibility to give the viewer "not only what they think they want, but what the artists know they will want once they try it and once they get to like it".
I have received hundreds of letters from viewers expressing disgust with the type of drama being presented in prime viewing time on CBC, and almost as many telephone calls. All but four of them support my position in this matter. Other members, perhaps all members of this House, have also received letters from constituents, and I believe the CBC has been deluged with complaints.
Some people have sent me copies of a form letter sent out by CBC and headed "Dear Viewer". This indicates to me that the corporation does not take these complaints seriously. Why should it, Madam Speaker, when its own minister states publicly that he does not intend to instruct the network? The form letter tells the recipient that the author of the book "Ten Lost Years" was satisfied with the television adaptation.
I have to agree with a letter I received from the president of a local Council of Women in which she asks the question: whose rights are we supposed to protect, those of the parents and the decent citizens, or those of the smut peddlers? I have received many letters from people who lived through the depression years and every one of them states that the program was not a true presentation of that era; they say that the filth and pornography portrayed in the program only degraded the people and undermined their fine efforts to get through a serious depression.
It has been suggested that anyone who does not want to hear vulgar language or see pornography on television can turn the dial or turn off the set. What an irresponsible thing to suggest. There are people in parts of this country

who only have access to two channels on television, and there are some places where there is only one channel. Why should people who pay to support the CBC be told that if they do not like to watch filth and garbage on their screens they can turn it off?
The CBC must be told immediately to clean up broadcasting in this country. This year the corporation is asking for $352 million in public money. That is a lot of money. It belongs to the Canadian people, and someone in the cabinet has to accept responsibility for the way in which it is spent. This is not a request. It is a basic necessity.

Mr. Gustave Blouin (Parliamentary Secretary to
Secretary of State): Madam Speaker, further to what the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott) has just told us, and more specifically to the question he put to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) on February 12 last, I wish to assure the House that when an hon. member asks the CBC for a tape recording of a program heard over the waves reserved for its broadcasts, usually the CBC accedes to his request. Almost invariably, the tapes requested deal with information, documentaries or current affairs programs; the CBC supplies this type of tapes every year to a great many hon. members.
Adjournment Debate
However, with regard to plays televised by the CBC, they fall into a somewhat different category. The CBC feels that they form a whole, where sound and image cannot be dissociated, if the whole is to keep its artistic value. Thus sound and picture must go together if a fair and honest assessment is to be made.
For the above reason, Madam Speaker, it has been the established practice of the corporation to organize for members a screening of a program which they would like to see again. Quite recently, for example, some members attended, at their request, a screening of the drama entitled "Heads, Guts and Sound Bone Dance" which was shown by the CBC last year.
The CBC has already let it known, Madam Speaker, that it is still prepared to show to the members concerned the telecast "Ten Lost Years" to which the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton referred in the House on February 12. You can be sure that as soon as the transcription is available, an official of the CBC will communicate with the members who have indicated that they would like to see that program again.
